units.intro: This unit is about six parts of the human body: the digestive, respiratory, circulatory, reproductive and skeletal systems, and homeostasis.

cards.title: Taking food in
body: Putting food into the mouth is called **ingestion**.
Our body cells cannot use big pieces of food. Food must become simple and small first.

cards.title: What is digestion?
body: **Digestion** is breaking down big food into simple, soluble forms.
Soluble means it can dissolve.
These small parts can enter the body cells and be used.

cards.title: Big or small?
body: Look at the picture. Move the slider.

states.label: Big piece
states.text: A big piece cannot pass through a small opening.

states.label: Small pieces
states.text: Break it into small pieces. Now they can pass. Food must also become small to enter the cells.

cards.title: Two phases of digestion
body: Digestion has two phases:
- **Mechanical phase**: food is broken into smaller pieces. It is only a physical change. It begins in the mouth.
- **Chemical phase**: big food substances become the smallest substances. **Enzymes** from digestive glands do this.

cards.title: Remember this
body: Mechanical = make small pieces (like teeth chewing).
Chemical = enzymes change the food.
Small pieces help the chemical phase to work.

cards.title: The food tube
body: The organs of digestion make a food tube. It is called the **alimentary canal**.
Tap the dots to see the names.

cards.title: Memory trick: order of the food tube
body: Say it three times: **My Eager Sister Sells Lemons Right Away**.

cards.title: Digestive glands
body: The digestive system also has **digestive glands**.
They pour digestive juice into the alimentary canal.
Examples: the **salivary glands**, the **liver** and the **pancreas**.

cards.title: A very long tube
body: The alimentary canal is about **9 metres** long.
But an adult is only about 1.7 metres tall!

cards.title: In the mouth
body: Both phases of digestion start in the **mouth**.
The teeth chew the food.
The tongue mixes food with **saliva**.
Saliva has an enzyme. It changes starch into simple sugar.
Saliva also makes food wet and slippery. So we swallow it easily.

cards.title: The tongue
body: The tongue is an organ of taste. It also:
- keeps food between the teeth for chewing,
- rolls the food and pushes it to the back of the mouth,
- helps us to speak.
Then food goes down the **esophagus**. It is a narrow muscular tube from the mouth to the stomach.

cards.title: Two sets of teeth
body: Humans have two sets of teeth in life:
- **Milk teeth** (temporary teeth) grow first, when we are young.
- **Permanent teeth** replace the milk teeth in childhood. By age 18, most people have **32** permanent teeth.
Permanent teeth are not replaced if they are lost.

cards.title: Four types of teeth
body: Move the slider to see each type.

states.label: Incisors
states.text: **8 incisors** (4 up, 4 down). Front teeth with sharp edges. For **biting and cutting**.

states.label: Canines
states.text: **4 canines** (2 up, 2 down). Sharp points. For **tearing and piercing**.

states.label: Premolars
states.text: **8 premolars** (4 up, 4 down). Broad, with round bumps. For **crushing and grinding**.

states.label: Molars
states.text: **12 molars** (6 up, 6 down). Broad, for **crushing and grinding**. Molars are only in the permanent set.

cards.title: Memory trick: teeth jobs
body: Front to back: **I Can Press More**.
Numbers: 8 + 4 + 8 + 12 = 32 teeth.

cards.title: Tooth decay
body: If you do not clean your teeth, **plaque** forms. Plaque is a sticky film with bacteria.
Bacteria change sugar into acids. Acids dissolve the hard surface of the teeth. This is tooth decay.
To stop decay:
- eat as little sugar as possible,
- brush your teeth regularly,
- visit a dentist for a check up.

cards.title: The stomach
body: The **stomach** is a bag with thick muscular walls.
Food stays there for about **1 to 3 hours**.
Glands in its wall make **gastric juice**. Its enzymes digest **proteins**.
The walls squeeze and mix the food. Then food goes to the small intestine, a little at a time.

cards.title: Small intestine: three juices
body: The **small intestine** is a tube about **6 metres** long. Three juices help here:
- **Bile** comes from the liver. It is green. It is stored in the gallbladder. Bile has **no enzyme**. Its salts help to break up fats.
- **Pancreatic juice** comes from the pancreas. It has three enzymes: for carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
- **Intestinal juice** comes from the wall of the intestine. It finishes the digestion.

cards.title: Bile is special
body: Bile has **NO enzyme**.
It only helps with fats (mechanical digestion of fats).
Remember it well!

cards.title: Absorption
body: Digested food is simple and soluble. It passes through the wall of the small intestine into the blood.
This is called **absorption**.
The blood carries the food to all living cells.
Food that is not digested goes on to the large intestine.

cards.title: Large intestine and egestion
body: The **large intestine** is about **1.5 metres** long. It has two parts: the colon and the rectum.
Here much water goes back into the blood. So the waste (faeces) becomes more solid.
Faeces are stored in the **rectum**. They leave through the **anus**. This is **egestion**.

steps.text: **Mouth**: teeth chew. Saliva starts to digest starch.
**Esophagus**: the food goes down this tube.
**Stomach**: gastric juice digests proteins. Food stays 1 to 3 hours.
**Small intestine**: bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice finish digestion. Food is absorbed into the blood.
**Large intestine**: water goes back into the blood.
**Rectum and anus**: faeces are stored, then pass out (egestion).

cards.title: Four words in order
body: **In** → ingestion (food goes in)
**Down** → digestion (food breaks down)
**Across** → absorption (food goes across the wall into blood)
**Exit** → egestion (waste goes out)

cards.q: Which digestive juice has no enzyme?
cards.why: Bile has no enzyme. Its salts only help to break up fats.

cards.title: Energy from food
body: We need energy for every activity: to grow, to move, to reproduce.
We get this energy from food.
**Respiration** is the chemical reaction that releases energy from food. It happens in living cells.

cards.title: The respiration equation
body: Respiration can be written like this:
$$\begin{aligned}&\text{Food} + \text{Oxygen}\\ \rightarrow\ &\text{Carbon dioxide} + \text{Water}\\ +\ &\text{Energy}\end{aligned}$$
Oxygen goes in. Carbon dioxide, water and energy come out.

cards.title: Breathing
body: **Oxygen** is a gas in the air. It is vital for life. Without oxygen our body cells die.
**Breathing** is the mechanical process that takes air into the body and out of the body.
Air with oxygen comes in. Air with waste carbon dioxide goes out.

cards.title: Breathing is not respiration
body: **Breathing** moves air in and out.
**Respiration** releases energy from food in the cells.
Do not mix them up!

cards.title: Organs of breathing
body: The respiratory system has the **nose**, the **trachea** and the **lungs**.
Tap the dots to see all the parts.

cards.title: The nose
body: The nose has two openings: the **nostrils**. They lead to the **nasal passage**.
Sticky mucus and hairs in the nasal passage filter the air. They remove dust and germs. We sneeze them out.
The nasal passage also warms the air and makes it moist.
So it is better to breathe in through the nose than through the mouth.

cards.title: The trachea (windpipe)
body: Clean, warm air goes into the **pharynx** (throat). Then it goes into the **trachea**.
The trachea is a tube that carries air to the lungs.
Its top part is the **larynx** (voice box, or Adam's apple).
The opening of the trachea is the **glottis**. Above it is the **epiglottis**. The epiglottis stops food from going into the windpipe.

cards.title: Bronchi and bronchioles
body: At its lower end, the trachea divides into two tubes: the **bronchi**.
One bronchus goes into the right lung. One goes into the left lung.
Inside the lungs, each bronchus divides into many small branches: the **bronchioles**.

cards.title: The lungs
body: The two lungs are in the chest cavity (**thorax**). The heart is there too.
The floor of the chest cavity is a sheet of muscle: the **diaphragm**.
The lungs are large and spongy. The ribs, chest muscles and diaphragm close them in.
Each bronchiole ends in a group of air sacs: the **alveoli**. Each alveolus has many tiny blood capillaries around it.
The alveoli are the true breathing surface of the lungs.

steps.text: Air comes in through the **nostrils**.
The **nasal passage** cleans, warms and wets the air.
The air goes through the **pharynx** (throat).
It goes down the **trachea** (windpipe).
The trachea divides into two **bronchi**.
Each bronchus divides into **bronchioles**.
The air reaches the air sacs: the **alveoli**.

cards.title: Memory trick: path of air
body: **Never Put Ten Big Bananas Anywhere!**

steps.text: Breathed-in air reaches the air sac. It has **a lot of oxygen** and little carbon dioxide.
Oxygen **dissolves** in the moist surface of the air sac.
The oxygen passes through the **thin wall** into the blood capillary.
The blood **carries the oxygen** to all the body cells.
Blood brings **carbon dioxide** from the cells. It passes from the blood into the air sac.
So breathed-out air has **more carbon dioxide** and less oxygen.

cards.title: Breathing in and out
body: Move the slider. Watch the chest, the lungs and the diaphragm.

states.label: Breathe in
states.text: The chest wall **rises**. The diaphragm pushes **down**. The lungs get **bigger**. Air comes in.

states.label: Breathe out
states.text: The chest wall **lowers**. The diaphragm pushes **up**. The lungs get **smaller**. Air is pushed out.

cards.title: Easy rule
body: Breathe **IN**: diaphragm **down**, lungs **big**.
Breathe **OUT**: diaphragm **up**, lungs **small**.
In the model with a bell jar (Figure 1.6), the balloons are like the lungs. The rubber sheet is like the diaphragm.

cards.q: Which part stops food from going into the windpipe?
cards.why: The epiglottis is above the glottis. It stops food from entering the windpipe.

cards.title: Why do we need circulation?
body: Living things need a circulatory system for two main reasons:
1. to carry food (nutrients), oxygen and other useful things to all body cells,
2. to remove wastes made by the cells.

cards.title: Three parts
body: The human circulatory system has three parts:
- the **blood**,
- the **blood vessels**,
- the **heart**.

cards.title: What is blood?
body: Blood is a fluid tissue. It has a liquid part, the **plasma**, and a solid part, the **blood cells**.
An adult has about **5 litres** of blood. **55%** is plasma. **45%** is blood cells.

cards.title: Red blood cells
body: There are about **5 million** red blood cells in each cubic millimetre of blood.
They **carry oxygen** from the lungs to the body tissues.
They have **hemoglobin**. Hemoglobin contains iron.
Red blood cells are made in the **bone marrow**.
If food has too little iron, the body makes too little hemoglobin. Then the blood cannot carry enough oxygen.

cards.title: White blood cells
body: White blood cells have **no hemoglobin**.
Most of them are made in the bone marrow.
There are about **7,000 to 10,000** in each cubic millimetre of blood.
Their job: to **defend the body against germs** that cause disease.

cards.title: Platelets
body: Platelets are made in the bone marrow. They are much smaller than red or white blood cells.
There are about **250,000** in each cubic millimetre of blood.
Their main job: to help the blood to **clot**.
When skin is cut, platelets clump together at the wound. The clot stops more bleeding. It also stops germs from getting in.

cards.title: Memory trick: blood cell jobs
body: **Red Runs with oxygen. White Wins against germs. Platelets Patch the cut.**

cards.title: Arteries
body: **Arteries** get blood straight from the heart. They carry it **away** to all body organs.
The largest artery is the **aorta**. In each organ, arteries divide into the smallest arteries: **arterioles**.
Blood in arteries flows **fast** and at **high pressure**. So artery walls are **thick, muscular and elastic**.

cards.title: Veins
body: **Veins** carry blood from the body organs **back to the heart**.
Tiny veins (**venules**) join to make bigger veins.
Blood enters the heart through the two largest veins: the **upper vena cava** and the **lower vena cava**.
Blood in veins flows **slowly** and at **low pressure**. Vein walls are **thinner**, less muscular and less elastic.

cards.title: Capillaries
body: **Capillaries** are the tiniest blood vessels. There are more of them than any other vessel.
They are microscopic, with very thin walls. They are between the cells of every organ.
They connect arterioles to venules.
Useful things and wastes pass between the blood and the cells through capillary walls.

cards.title: Artery, vein, capillary
body: Compare the walls.

cards.title: A for Away
body: **A**rtery = **A**way from the heart.
**V**ein = back to the heart (think: **V**isit home).

cards.title: The heart
body: The **heart** is a muscular organ. It pumps blood around the body.
It is about the size of a closed fist. It is in the chest, between the two lungs.
It has **four chambers**:
- two thin-walled upper chambers: the **auricles**,
- two thick-walled lower chambers: the **ventricles**.
We call them left and right.

cards.title: Inside the heart
body: Tap the dots to see the parts.
The picture shows the heart as if you face the person. So the person's right side is on your left.

cards.title: Path of blood through the heart

steps.text: Blood from all body parts enters the **right auricle** through the two **venae cavae**.
The right auricle fills and contracts. Blood goes into the **right ventricle**.
The right ventricle contracts. Blood goes into the **pulmonary artery**, to the **lungs**.
Blood comes back from the lungs through the **pulmonary veins** into the **left auricle**.
The left auricle contracts. Blood goes into the **left ventricle**.
The left ventricle pushes blood with much force into the **aorta**. The aorta carries it to all parts of the body.
**Valves** are between the auricles and the ventricles. They close when the ventricles contract. So blood cannot go back.

cards.title: Right to lungs, left to body
body: The **right** side of the heart sends blood to the **lungs**.
The **left** side sends blood to the **whole body** (through the aorta).
**A**uricles are on top, **V**entricles are below. A comes before V.

cards.q: Which chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
cards.why: The left ventricle contracts and pushes blood into the aorta.

cards.title: The male system
body: The male reproductive system has:
- the **penis**,
- a pair of **testes** with their tubes,
- the male reproductive **glands**.

cards.title: Puberty in boys
body: At **puberty**, the testes start to make the **male sex hormone**.
This hormone makes the testes produce **sperm**.
Each testis has many twisted tubules. Sperm are made there.
Once the testes start making sperm, they go on for the rest of life.

cards.title: Path of sperm
body: Sperm pass from the tubules into a **sperm duct**. The two sperm ducts join just below the urinary bladder. This tube is the **urethra**.
The urethra runs through the penis to the outside. Both urine and sperm leave the body through it.

cards.title: Semen
body: The male glands make a thick fluid: **seminal fluid**.
It has food for the sperm. It helps them to swim.
Sperm + seminal fluid = **semen**.

cards.title: Changes in boys
body: The male sex hormone also brings these changes:
- hair grows on the face, around the sex organ and in the armpits,
- the voice box gets larger, and the voice becomes deeper,
- the sex organs grow larger and start making sperm,
- the body shape changes slowly as bones and muscles grow.

cards.title: The female system
body: The female reproductive system has a **vagina**, a **uterus**, and a pair of **ovaries** with two **fallopian tubes**.
Tap the dots to see the parts.

cards.title: How the parts connect
body: Each ovary is connected to a **fallopian tube** (also called an **oviduct**).
The two tubes lead into the muscular **uterus** (womb).
A fertilized egg grows and develops in the uterus.
The uterus leads to the outside of the body through the vaginal canal.

cards.title: Puberty in girls
body: A baby girl is born with many thousands of unripe eggs in her ovaries.
At puberty, the ovaries start to make **female sex hormones**. These make the ovaries produce **ova** (eggs).
The hormones also bring changes:
- the breasts become larger,
- hair grows under the armpits and in the groin,
- fat develops around the hips, bottom and thighs,
- the reproductive organs prepare for reproduction.

steps.text: About every **28 days**, one egg ripens in an ovary.
The egg is released from the ovary. This is **ovulation**.
If there are sperm, the egg is probably fertilized. This usually happens in the **fallopian tube**. The fertilized egg is a **zygote**.
The zygote enters the **uterus**. It attaches to the thick wall. The female is now pregnant.
If the egg is **not** fertilized, it passes out through the vagina with some blood from the uterus. This is **menstruation**.

cards.title: Menopause
body: Ovulation normally goes on until **menopause**. This is usually at **45 to 50 years** of age.
Menopause is the stage when a female stops ovulation.

cards.title: Memory trick: egg words

letters.m: ovulation: egg comes out of the ovary
menstruation: unfertilized egg leaves with blood

body: **menoPAUSE** has the word **pause** in it: ovulation stops.

cards.title: Where does it happen?
body: **Fertilization** usually happens in the **fallopian tube**.
The baby grows in the **uterus**.
Sperm and urine both leave through the **urethra** (in males).

cards.title: Parts of the skeleton
body: The skeletal system has **bones**, **cartilages** and **ligaments**.
There are **206 bones** in the human body.
The size and shape of each bone is closely related to its job (function).

cards.title: Cartilage and ligaments
body: **Cartilage** is softer and more slippery than bone. It is at the ends of many bones, mostly at joints.
Cartilage reduces friction when bones move past each other.
**Ligaments** are strong bands of elastic tissue. They tie bones to one another.

cards.title: The human skeleton
body: Tap the dots to see the names of the bones.

cards.title: Five jobs of the skeleton
body: The skeleton:
1. gives **support and shape** to the body,
2. allows **movement** and locomotion,
3. **protects** soft organs inside the body,
4. **produces** red blood cells and some white blood cells,
5. **stores minerals**, mainly calcium and phosphate salts.

cards.title: Memory trick: five jobs
body: **Strong Men Protect Blood Stores.**

cards.title: Three main parts
body: The textbook divides the skeleton into three main parts:
1. the **axial skeleton**,
2. the **appendicular skeleton**,
3. the **breastbone and ribs**.

cards.title: The axial skeleton
body: It has the **skull** and the **spinal column** (backbone).
The skull has the **cranium** and the jaws. The cranium protects the brain and the main sense organs.
The spinal column is made of separate bones: the **vertebrae**. Ligaments join them end to end. Cartilages separate them.
The spinal column gives flexible support. It protects the **spinal cord**.

cards.title: The appendicular skeleton
body: It has the **pectoral girdle** with the arms, and the **hip girdle** with the legs.
A **girdle** is a ring of bones. It connects the arms or legs to the spinal column.
- Arms attach to the **pectoral (shoulder) girdle**.
- Legs attach to the **pelvic (hip) girdle**.

cards.title: The breastbone and ribs
body: The **breastbone** is a flat bone. The collarbones and the rib bones are connected to it.
The ribs and the breastbone make the **thoracic cavity**.
This cavity protects the **heart and the lungs**.

cards.title: Bones, muscles and joints
body: Bones and muscles work together to make movement.
Bones move when muscles **contract and relax**.
A **joint** is the point where two bones meet.
Some joints move a lot. Some move a little. Some do not move at all.

cards.title: Five kinds of joints
body: Move the slider to see each joint.

states.label: Ball and socket
states.text: **Ball and socket joint**: in the hip and shoulder. It moves **freely in all directions**.

states.label: Hinge
states.text: **Hinge joint**: in the elbow, knee and fingers. It moves in **one plane only**, like a door hinge.

states.label: Gliding
states.text: **Gliding joint**: in the bones of the hands, feet and the vertebrae. It allows only **slight movement**.

states.label: Fixed
states.text: **Fixed joint**: between the bones of the cranium. It allows **no movement**.

states.label: Pivot
states.text: **Pivot joint**: between the head and the vertebrae. It allows **nodding and turning**.

cards.title: Picture words
body: **Door** → hinge
**Ball in a cup** → ball and socket
**Sliding** → gliding
**Locked** → fixed
**Turning head** → pivot

cards.q: Strong bands of elastic tissue that tie bones together are called:
cards.why: Ligaments are strong bands of elastic tissue that bind bones to one another.

cards.title: What is homeostasis?
body: Living things must notice changes outside and inside the body. Then they must respond.
Keeping the inside of the body fairly constant is called **homeostasis**.
It gives the best conditions for the body tissues to work well.
The parts of the body must work together (in harmony) to keep homeostasis.

cards.title: Cold-blooded and warm-blooded
body: **Fishes, amphibians and reptiles**: their body temperature changes with the surroundings. Hot day, hot body. Cold day, cold body.
They are **poikilothermic** (cold-blooded) animals.
**Birds and mammals** keep their body temperature constant.
They are **homoeothermic** (warm-blooded) animals.

cards.title: Memory trick: cold or warm blood?
body: **F-A-R**: for fishes, amphibians and reptiles, the body temperature goes far up and far down with the weather.
**Birds and mammals** keep it the same. **Homoeo** sounds like **home**: always the same.

cards.title: The brain controls body heat
body: Receptors in the brain check the temperature of the blood.
Nerves also tell the brain about the temperature of the skin.
The brain controls temperature regulation.
Human body temperature is kept at **37 °C**. The **skin** helps to keep it constant.

cards.title: Too hot or too cold?
body: Move the slider. Watch the hairs, the sweat and the blood vessel.

states.label: Too cold
states.text:
- **Sweating stops**, so little heat is lost.
- Blood vessels **narrow**. Less blood flows near the skin.
- Hairs **stand up**. More air is trapped. It stops heat loss.
- **Shivering**: muscles contract and relax fast. This makes more heat.

states.label: Normal
states.text: The body temperature is **37 °C**. The skin keeps it constant.

states.label: Too hot
states.text:
- **Sweating** happens. Sweat evaporates and removes heat.
- Blood vessels near the skin **widen**. More heat is lost through the skin.
- Hairs **lie flat**. Less air is trapped, so heat is lost easily.

cards.title: Hot or cold: what the body does
head: Too hot (heat gain)
Too cold (heat loss)

cards.title: Shivering is only for cold
body: **Shivering** makes heat. It happens only when we are **too cold**.
**Sweating** removes heat. It happens when we are **too hot**.

cards.title: Water balance
body: The body loses water as vapour, sweat and urine.
But the amount of water in the blood must stay constant.
The **skin** and the **kidneys** are very important for water balance.

cards.title: Drink little or drink a lot?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Drink little
states.text: The blood has less water. The brain notices the shortage. The kidneys **keep water** in the body. So **less urine** comes out. It is **yellowish** and has a very bad smell.

states.label: Drink a lot
states.text: The blood has more water. The brain notices the extra water. The kidneys **pass the extra water** out. So **more urine** comes out. It is **colourless** and has less smell.

cards.title: Little in, little out
body: Little water in → **little** urine out, **yellow** and smelly.
Lots of water in → **lots of** urine out, **clear**, less smell.

cards.q: Which of these helps the body when it is too cold?
cards.why: Shivering makes extra heat. The other three help the body to lose heat.

tips.text: Learn the **paths** as a chain: food (mouth → anus), air (nose → alveoli), blood (right auricle → … → aorta). Draw arrows in your book.
Learn **opposite pairs** together: artery / vein, breathe in / breathe out, too hot / too cold, drink little / drink a lot.
Know the **singular and plural**: bronchus → bronchi, alveolus → alveoli, ovum → ova, testis → testes, vena cava → venae cavae.
Numbers to know: **9 m** food tube, **6 m** small intestine, **1.5 m** large intestine, **32** teeth, **5 litres** of blood, **206** bones, **37 °C**, **28** days.
Read the question slowly. Look for **not** and **except**. Example: "Which is **not** an organ of the respiratory system?"
Options like **"A and C"** or **"all of the above"**: check each option one by one first.
**Breathing ≠ respiration.** Breathing moves air. Respiration releases energy from food in the cells.

Veins carry blood away from the heart.
items.why: Arteries carry blood away. Veins bring it back.

items.text: Red blood cells defend the body against germs.
items.why: White blood cells do that. Red cells carry oxygen.

items.text: Fertilization usually happens in the uterus.
items.why: It usually happens in the fallopian tube.

items.text: There are 206 bones in the human body.

items.why: Birds and mammals are warm-blooded (homoeothermic).

items.text: Shivering happens when we are too cold.

questions.q: Putting food into the mouth is called:
why: Ingestion means taking food **in**, into the mouth.
Digestion breaks food down. Absorption takes food into the blood. Egestion passes waste out.
questions.tip: Remember the chain: **In → Down → Across → Exit** (ingestion → digestion → absorption → egestion).

similar.q: Passing out undigested food through the anus is called ___.

questions.q: Where do both mechanical and chemical digestion start?
why: In the mouth, teeth chew food: this is mechanical digestion.
Saliva has an enzyme that digests starch: this is chemical digestion.
So both start in the mouth.
questions.tip: Ask: where does food meet teeth AND an enzyme first?

similar.q: Which organ stores food for about 1 to 3 hours?

questions.q: Bile contains enzymes that digest fats.
why: Bile has **no** enzyme.
Its salts only help the mechanical digestion of fats.
questions.tip: Words like "contains enzymes" are a trap for bile. Bile = no enzyme.

similar.q: True or false: pancreatic juice has three enzymes.

questions.q: An adult has ___ permanent teeth.
why: Count the four types: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, 12 molars.
questions.tip: Chunk the numbers: 8, 4, 8, 12. Add them in small steps: 8 + 4 = 12, then 8 + 12 = 20, then 12 + 20 = 32.

similar.q: How many molars are in the upper jaw?

questions.q: Food + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. This equation shows:
why: Energy is released from food. This is **respiration**.
Breathing only moves air in and out.
questions.tip: See the word **Energy** at the end? Think respiration.

similar.q: What do we call moving air into and out of the body?

questions.q: Which part stops food from entering the windpipe?
why: The epiglottis is above the glottis (the opening of the trachea).
It stops food from going into the windpipe.
questions.tip: **Epi**glottis sits on top (like a lid) of the glottis.

similar.q: Which part is called the voice box?

questions.q: When you breathe in, the diaphragm pushes down and the lungs get bigger.
why: Breathing in: the chest wall rises, the diaphragm pushes down, the lungs get bigger, air comes in.
questions.tip: IN = down and big. OUT = up and small.

similar.q: True or false: when you breathe out, the lungs get bigger.

questions.q: Which blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the body?
why: Red blood cells have hemoglobin.
Their job is to carry oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues.
questions.tip: Red **R**uns with oxygen. White **W**ins against germs. Platelets **P**atch the cut.

similar.q: Which blood cells help the blood to clot?

questions.q: Blood vessels that carry blood back to the heart are called ___.
why: Arteries carry blood **away** from the heart.
Veins carry blood **back** to the heart.
questions.tip: **A** for **A**way (artery). The other one (vein) comes back.

similar.q: What is the largest artery called?

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood into the aorta?
why: The left auricle sends blood to the left ventricle.
The left ventricle contracts with much force and pushes blood into the aorta.
The aorta carries blood to all the body.
questions.tip: Right side → lungs. Left side → body. Ventricles pump out of the heart.

similar.q: Which chamber receives blood from the two venae cavae?

questions.q: The release of an egg from an ovary about every 28 days is called:
why: When the egg leaves the **ov**ary, it is **ov**ulation.
Menstruation is when an unfertilized egg passes out with blood. Menopause is when ovulation stops.
questions.tip: Match the start of the word: **ov**ary → **ov**ulation.

similar.q: What is the stage when a female stops ovulation?

questions.q: The joints in the elbow, knee and fingers are ___ joints.
why: These joints move in one plane only, like the hinge of a door.
So they are hinge joints.
questions.tip: Picture a door opening and closing. That is the elbow.

similar.q: What kind of joints are between the bones of the cranium?

questions.q: Shivering helps the body when it is too hot.
why: Shivering makes extra heat: muscles contract and relax fast.
So it happens when we are too **cold**, not too hot.
questions.tip: Ask: does this make heat or lose heat? Making heat is for cold.

similar.q: True or false: sweating stops when we get too cold.

questions.q: You drink very little water on a hot day. What happens to your urine? Why?
questions.answer: Less urine comes out. It is yellowish and has a very bad smell. This is because the blood has less water. The brain notices this, and the kidneys keep water in the body.
why: Little water in the blood → the brain detects the shortage.
The kidneys keep (retain) water.
So less urine comes out. It is yellowish, with a bad smell.
questions.tip: Answer in two parts: **what** happens (less, yellow urine) and **why** (kidneys keep water).

similar.q: What happens to your urine if you drink a lot of water?
similar.a: More urine comes out. It is colourless and has less smell.

questions.q: Write three jobs of the skeleton.
questions.answer: Any three of these: it gives support and shape; it allows movement; it protects organs inside the body; it produces red blood cells and some white blood cells; it stores minerals (calcium and phosphate).
why: The textbook lists five jobs of the skeleton.
Any three of the five are correct.
questions.tip: Use the memory trick: **Strong Men Protect Blood Stores** (support, movement, protection, blood cells, storage).

similar.q: Which part of the skeleton protects the heart and the lungs?
similar.a: the ribs and the breastbone (the thoracic cavity)

units.title: Force and Motion
units.intro: This unit is about forces and motion: combining forces, balanced and unbalanced forces, displacement, velocity, acceleration, and Newton's second and third laws.

u2velocity.title: Constant velocity and change of velocity

u2accel.title: A car with an acceleration of 5 m/s²

cards.title: Many forces at once
body: Two or more forces can act on an object at the same time.
Example: three pupils pull a large box in different directions (Figure 2.1). Three forces act on the box.
We can put these forces together. We get **one single force**. It has the same effect as the three forces.

cards.title: What is a net force?
body: A **net force** ($F_n$) is the combination of all the forces acting on an object.
In Grade 8 you learn two cases:
- forces along the **same line**,
- forces at a **right angle**.

cards.title: Three ways to combine
body: Move the slider. Look at the red arrow: it is the net force.

states.label: Same direction
states.text: Two pupils push a wagon the **same way**: 600 N and 500 N. **Add** them. Net force = **1100 N**, in the same direction.

states.label: Opposite
states.text: Two pupils push **opposite ways**: 600 N and 500 N. **Subtract**. Net force = **100 N**, in the direction of the bigger force.

states.label: Right angle
states.text: 300 N north and 400 N east. Use **Pythagoras**. Net force = **500 N**. Its direction is between the two forces.

cards.title: Same direction: add
body: If two forces are in the **same direction**, add them.
Example: $F_n = 600\text{ N} + 500\text{ N} = 1100\text{ N}$
The net force is in the same direction as the two forces.

cards.title: Opposite directions: subtract
body: If two forces are in **opposite directions**, the net force is the **difference**.
Example: $F_n = 600\text{ N} - 500\text{ N} = 100\text{ N}$
The net force is in the direction of the **larger** force.

cards.title: Right angle: Pythagoras
body: If two forces act at a **right angle**, use the **Pythagoras Theorem** to find the size.
The direction of the net force is **between** the two forces.

cards.title: Worked example: 300 N and 400 N
body: Two pupils pull with 300 N north and 400 N east.

cards.title: Memory trick: S-O-R

letters.m: opposite: subtract, the bigger force wins

body: First ask: **Same? Opposite? Right angle?** Then choose the rule.
Remember 3, 4, 5: forces of 3 N and 4 N at a right angle give 5 N.

cards.title: Tug of war
body: Look at Activity 2.1 B. Team A pulls with **5000 N**. Team B pulls with **4500 N**.
The two forces are in **opposite** directions.
Net force = 5000 N − 4500 N = **500 N**, in the direction of team A.
The net force is not zero, so the rope moves towards team A.

cards.title: Biggest and smallest
body: Two forces give the **biggest** net force when they act in the **same** direction.
They give the **smallest** net force when they act in **opposite** directions.
Example: 3 N and 4 N give 7 N (same), 1 N (opposite), 5 N (right angle).

cards.q: Forces of 10 N and 15 N act in the same direction. The net force is:
cards.why: Same direction: add. 10 N + 15 N = 25 N.

cards.title: Balanced forces
body: Forces are **balanced** if their effects **cancel** each other.
Then the net force is **zero**.
Balanced forces cause **no change** in motion:
- an object at rest **stays at rest**,
- a moving object **keeps on moving**.

cards.title: Unbalanced forces
body: Forces are **unbalanced** if their effects do **not** cancel.
Then the net force is **not zero**.
Unbalanced forces can **change** the motion:
- an object at rest may **start** to move,
- a moving object may **speed up**, **slow down** or **come to rest**.

cards.title: Pushing a door
body: Two friends push a door from both sides (Activity 2.2). Move the slider.

states.label: Same push
states.text: Both push with the **same force** in opposite directions. The effects cancel. Net force = **0**. The door does **not** move. The forces are **balanced**.

states.label: One pushes harder
states.text: One friend pushes **harder**. The effects do not cancel. The net force is **not zero**. The door **moves** away from the bigger push. The forces are **unbalanced**.

cards.title: Balanced or unbalanced?
head: Balanced
Unbalanced
rows: speeds up, slows down or stops

cards.title: Example: four forces
body: Four forces act on an object: **10 N east**, **15 N south**, **10 N west** and **15 N north** (Exercise 2.2).
10 N east and 10 N west cancel.
15 N south and 15 N north cancel.
Net force = **0**. So the forces are **balanced**.

cards.title: Equal and opposite
body: Two **equal** forces in **opposite** directions are balanced.
An object with only these two forces stays at rest (or keeps moving).
**Balanced = zero net force = no change.**

cards.q: When the forces on an object are balanced, the net force is:
cards.why: Balanced forces cancel each other. So the net force is zero.

cards.title: What can an unbalanced force do?
body: An unbalanced force can change:
1. the **position** of an object,
2. the **speed** of an object,
3. the **direction of motion** of an object.

cards.title: Three effects
body: Move the slider to see each effect.

states.label: Position
states.text: You **kick** a football that is resting on the ground. It moves to a new place. Its **position** changes.

states.label: Speed
states.text: A boy pushes a girl on a wagon in the direction she is moving. She goes **faster**. Her **speed** changes.

states.label: Direction
states.text: You throw a ball at a wall. It strikes the wall and comes back. Its **direction** of motion changes.

cards.title: Faster or slower
body: Unbalanced forces can make a moving object go **faster**.
They can also make it **slow down** and **stop**.
Example: a push in the same direction as the motion makes the wagon go faster.

cards.title: Turning a car
body: A car cannot go round a curved path without changing direction.
The driver applies forces to turn the **steering wheel**. Then the car changes its direction of motion (Figure 2.10).

cards.title: How to slow down a wagon
body: A wagon moves east at a constant speed (Exercise 2.3).
To slow it down, push **against** the motion, towards the **west**.
Now the forces are unbalanced. The net force is opposite to the motion. So the wagon slows down.

cards.title: Memory trick: P-S-D
body: An unbalanced force says: **Please Stop Dancing!**
It changes **P**osition, **S**peed and **D**irection.

cards.q: A ball hits a wall and comes back. Which effect of an unbalanced force is this?
cards.why: The ball strikes the wall and changes its direction of motion.

cards.title: Distance and displacement
body: **Distance** is how far someone has travelled **following a path**.
**Displacement** is the change in position of an object. It is distance measured in a **straight line** and in a **particular direction**.

cards.title: Two ways to the library
body: You walk from your classroom (C) to the library (L) (Figure 2.11). Move the slider.

states.label: Path C → B → L
states.text: You go 400 m to B. Then 300 m to L. **Distance** = 400 m + 300 m = **700 m**.

states.label: Straight line C → L
states.text: The straight line from C to L is **500 m** long (Pythagoras: $400^2 + 300^2 = 500^2$). **Displacement** = **500 m** in the direction C → L.

cards.title: Tap the points
body: C is the start. L is the end.
Displacement only looks at the start and the end, and the direction.

cards.title: Why direction matters
body: Information about motion is not complete if you only give the distance.
You must give **distance and direction**.
A combination of distance and direction is **displacement**.

cards.title: Velocity
body: **Velocity** is the speed of an object in a particular direction.
It is also the **displacement per unit time**.
Example: a football player kicks a ball. He must guess the **speed** and the **direction** of the ball.

cards.title: Add a direction
body: Distance + **direction** = **displacement**
Speed + **direction** = **velocity**
So "20 km/h" is a speed. "20 km/h **north**" is a velocity.

cards.title: Constant or changing velocity?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Constant
states.text: The car goes **5 m every second** in a straight line. Speed 5 m/s in one direction. Its velocity is **constant** (uniform).

states.label: Changing
states.text: The car goes **60 km/h east**, then turns and goes **60 km/h north**. The speed is the same, but the **direction** changes. So the velocity **changes** (non-uniform).

cards.title: Constant velocity formula
body: When the velocity in one direction is constant:
$$\text{Displacement} = \text{velocity} \times \text{time}$$
$$s = v \times t$$

cards.title: When does velocity change?
body: Velocity changes if:
- the **speed** changes, or
- the **direction** changes, or
- **both** change.
Examples: buses speed up when they leave the bus stop. Trains slow down when they enter the station. Snails change direction as they crawl.

cards.title: Average velocity
body: Often velocity is not constant. Then we find the **average velocity**:
$$v_{ave} = \frac{s}{t} = \frac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time taken}}$$
Units: metre per second (**m/s**), kilometre per hour (**km/h**).

cards.title: Worked example 1
body: An artist moves **5 m** to the left of the stage in **15 s**. Find his average velocity.
Given: $s = 5$ m, $t = 15$ s
$v_{ave} = \frac{5\text{ m}}{15\text{ s}} = \frac{1}{3}\text{ m/s} \approx 0.33\text{ m/s}$ (to the left)

cards.title: Worked example 2
body: A mountain bike goes at an average speed of **4 m/s** for **10 minutes**. How far does it go?
First change minutes to seconds: 10 min = 10 × 60 = **600 s**.
$s = v_{ave} \times t = 4\text{ m/s} \times 600\text{ s} = 2400\text{ m}$

cards.title: Same units!
body: Before you calculate, make the units match.
1 minute = 60 seconds. 1 hour = 60 minutes.
Example: 15 minutes = $\frac{1}{4}$ hour.

cards.q: "20 km/h north" is an example of:
cards.why: It has a speed (20 km/h) and a direction (north). Speed + direction = velocity.

cards.title: Acceleration in everyday life
body: In everyday language, acceleration means **speeding up**.
Example: a driver steps on the **accelerator pedal**. The car goes faster.

cards.title: Acceleration in science
body: In science, an object **accelerates** when its motion changes: the **speed** changes or the **direction** changes.
A car that **slows down** at the traffic light is **still accelerating**!

cards.title: The formula
body: **Acceleration** is the change of velocity per unit time.
$$a = \frac{\Delta v}{t} = \frac{\text{change in velocity}}{\text{time taken}}$$
The sign $\Delta$ means "change".
The SI unit is **metre per second squared** (m/s²).

cards.title: A car with 5 m/s²

steps.text: After **1 second** the car moves at **5 m/s**.
After **2 seconds**: **10 m/s**. The velocity went up by 5 m/s.
After **3 seconds**: **15 m/s**. Again +5 m/s. The velocity changes by 5 m/s **every second**: acceleration = **5 m/s²**.

body: Tap Next. Watch the speed grow.

cards.title: Constant acceleration
body: An object has a **constant acceleration** if its velocity changes by **equal amounts** in **equal times**.
The car in Figure 2.13 has a constant acceleration of 5 m/s².

cards.title: Acceleration has a direction
body: - **Speeding up**: the acceleration is in the **same** direction as the motion.
- **Slowing down**: the acceleration is **opposite** to the motion.
Slowing down is also called **deceleration** or **negative acceleration**.

cards.title: Worked example: a train
body: A train goes from **10 m/s** to **25 m/s** in **3 s**. Find its acceleration.
$a = \frac{15\text{ m/s}}{3\text{ s}} = 5\text{ m/s}^2$

cards.title: Worked example: an eagle
body: An eagle accelerates downward at **4.6 m/s²** for **5 s**. Find the change in velocity.
$\Delta v = a \times t$
$\Delta v = 4.6\text{ m/s}^2 \times 5\text{ s} = 23\text{ m/s}$

cards.title: Memory trick: three ways to accelerate
body: **F-S-T**: Faster, Slower, Turn. All three are acceleration.
Not moving at all? No acceleration.

cards.q: Which is NOT an example of acceleration?

options.B: a dog running faster and faster
options.C: a man sitting at a street corner

cards.why: A man sitting still has no change in speed or direction. So there is no acceleration.

cards.title: Empty or full cupboard?
body: You push an empty cupboard and a cupboard full of clothes.
Which is easier to move? Think about it.
Newton found a rule that links **force**, **mass** and **acceleration**.

cards.title: Bricks on a roller
body: Activity 2.6: pull the roller with a spring balance. Move the slider.

states.label: 1 brick, force F
states.text: One brick, pulled with force F. The roller accelerates.

states.label: 2 bricks, force F
states.text: Two bricks (more mass), the **same** force F. The acceleration is **smaller**. More mass → less acceleration.

states.label: 2 bricks, force 2F
states.text: Two bricks, **twice** the force (2F). The acceleration is **bigger** again. More force → more acceleration.

cards.title: The set-up
body: Tap the dots to see the parts of the activity.

cards.title: Newton's two findings
body: Unbalanced forces give a **net force**. The net force makes the object accelerate or decelerate.
Newton found:
- the **bigger the force**, the **more** the object accelerates;
- the **heavier the mass**, the **less** it accelerates.

cards.title: Newton's second law
body: The acceleration of an object is **directly proportional** to the net force on it.
It is **inversely proportional** to its mass.
$$F_n = m \times a$$
Net force = mass × acceleration.

cards.title: What is 1 newton?
body: **One newton (1 N)** is the force that gives a **1 kg** mass an acceleration of **1 m/s²**.
$$1\text{ N} = 1\text{ kg} \times 1\text{ m/s}^2$$

cards.title: The formula triangle
body: Cover the letter you want. Move the slider.

states.label: Find F
states.text: Cover **F**. You see m next to a: $F_n = m \times a$

states.label: Find m
states.text: Cover **m**. You see F over a: $m = \frac{F}{a}$

states.label: Find a
states.text: Cover **a**. You see F over m: $a = \frac{F_n}{m}$

cards.title: Worked example: a football
body: A goalkeeper pushes a **250 g** football with **10 N**. Find its acceleration.
Change grams to kilograms: 250 g = **0.250 kg**.
$a = \frac{F_n}{m} = \frac{10\text{ N}}{0.250\text{ kg}} = 40\text{ m/s}^2$

cards.title: Worked example: a car
body: A car of mass **2000 kg** accelerates at **2 m/s²**. What force does the engine give?
$F_n = m \times a = 2000\text{ kg} \times 2\text{ m/s}^2 = 4000\text{ N}$

cards.title: Worked example: find the mass
body: A force of **40 N** gives an object an acceleration of **2 m/s²**. Find the mass.
$m = \frac{F}{a} = \frac{40\text{ N}}{2\text{ m/s}^2} = 20\text{ kg}$

cards.title: Kilograms, not grams
body: In $F = ma$, the mass must be in **kilograms** (kg).
Force in **N**, acceleration in **m/s²**.

cards.q: A net force of 8 N acts on a 2 kg object. Its acceleration is:
cards.why: a = F ÷ m = 8 N ÷ 2 kg = 4 m/s².

cards.title: First and second laws
body: **Newton's first law**: if the forces on an object are **balanced**, it stays at rest or moves with constant velocity.
**Newton's second law**: if the forces are **unbalanced**, the object accelerates in the direction of the net force.

cards.title: Forces come in pairs
body: Newton noticed that forces always come in **pairs**.
The two forces are **equal in size** but **opposite in direction**.
He called them **action** and **reaction**.

cards.title: Newton's third law
body: **For every action there is an equal but opposite reaction.**
When one object pushes on a second object, the second object pushes back with a force of the **same size**.

cards.title: Action and reaction
body: Move the slider to see three examples.

states.label: Firing a gun
states.text: You push on the gun to fire the bullets. The bullets push on the gun with the **same size** force. So the gun pushes your shoulder **backward** (Figure 2.19).

states.label: Jumping
states.text: You push **down** on the ground. The ground pushes **up** on you. This upward force pushes you into the air.

states.label: Pushing a table
states.text: You push a table with **60 N**. The table pushes you back with **60 N**.

cards.title: Walking and jumping
body: You use action and reaction pairs all the time when you move.
Walking and jumping both use them.

cards.title: Worked example
body: You push a table with a force of 60 N. What force does the table put on you?
Action force = reaction force
60 N = **60 N**, in the opposite direction.

cards.title: Equal and opposite
body: Action and reaction are **always equal** in size.
They are **always opposite** in direction.
You push something → it pushes **you** back just as hard.

cards.title: Newton's laws at a glance
head: Law
What it says
rows: balanced forces: at rest stays at rest; moving keeps a constant velocity
every action has an equal but opposite reaction

cards.title: Memory trick: 1, 2, 3
body: **1 = still, 2 = F = ma, 3 = pairs.**

cards.q: You push a car at rest with 500 N. What force does the car put on you?
cards.why: Third law: the reaction is equal to the action. So 500 N.

glossary.meaning: the combination of all the forces acting on an object (Fn)
forces whose effects cancel; the net force is zero
forces whose effects do not cancel; the net force is not zero
how far someone travels following a path
change in position: straight-line distance in a particular direction
speed in a particular direction; displacement per unit time
displacement divided by the time taken
change of velocity per unit time; unit m/s²
acceleration when a moving object slows down (negative acceleration)
unit of force (N); 1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²
one force of a force pair
the equal and opposite force of a force pair

tips.text: For two forces, first ask: **same** direction (add), **opposite** (subtract), or **right angle** (Pythagoras)?
Write **Given**, **Required**, **Solution** like the textbook. Then check the **units** (N, kg, m/s, m/s²).
Change **minutes to seconds** and **grams to kilograms** before you use a formula.
**Constant speed** in a straight line means balanced forces: forwards forces = backwards forces.
A car that slows down or turns is **accelerating**. Only "no change" means no acceleration.
Third law answers are easy: the reaction is **the same number** of newtons as the action.
Learn the three formulas: $v = \frac{s}{t}$, $a = \frac{\Delta v}{t}$, $F_n = ma$.

items.why: In science, slowing down is also acceleration (deceleration).

items.text: The SI unit of acceleration is m/s.
items.why: It is m/s² (metre per second squared).

items.text: An acceleration of 5 m/s² means the velocity changes by 5 m/s every second.
A car turning at constant speed has no acceleration.
items.why: Its direction changes, so its velocity changes.

pairs.b: The table pushes you with 60 N.

pairs.b: The bullets push the gun backward.

pairs.b: The ground pushes up on you.

pairs.b: The wall pushes you with 100 N.

items.why: That is distance. Displacement is a straight line with a direction.

items.why: The heavier the mass, the less it accelerates.

questions.q: Two forces of 10 N each act on a box in opposite directions. The net force is:
why: Opposite directions: subtract.
$10\text{ N} - 10\text{ N} = 0\text{ N}$
The forces are balanced.
questions.tip: Equal and opposite forces always cancel: net force 0.

similar.q: Two forces of 60 N each act in the same direction. What is the net force?

questions.q: A lorry moves at a constant speed. Air friction and friction push backwards. The engine pushes forwards. Which set is correct? (air friction, friction, engine)
why: Constant speed means **no change** in motion, so the forces are **balanced**.
Forwards force = backwards forces.
A: 2000 N + 1000 N = 3000 N. This matches the engine force.
questions.tip: Constant speed → add the backward forces → they must equal the forward force.

similar.q: A box does not move. One pupil pushes it with 50 N to the east. What force stops it moving?
similar.a: 50 N to the west (the forces are balanced).

questions.q: Ali rides a bicycle. When are the forces on the bicycle balanced?
why: Balanced forces cause **no change** in motion.
Speeding up, slowing down and turning are all changes.
Only D (constant speed, straight on) has no change.
questions.tip: Turning is a change of direction. It is NOT balanced.

similar.q: A car speeds up. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced?

questions.q: "20 km/h north" is an example of:
why: 20 km/h is a speed.
North is a direction.
Speed + direction = velocity.
questions.tip: km/h with a direction → velocity. m with a direction → displacement.

similar.q: "500 m towards the library" is an example of ___.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an example of acceleration?

options.A: a leaf falling with constant acceleration
options.C: a dog running faster and faster
options.D: a beggar sitting at a corner of the street

why: Acceleration means the velocity changes (speed or direction).
A, B and C all change speed.
A person sitting still has no change. So D is not acceleration.
questions.tip: Look for the one with **no change** at all.

similar.q: Is a car turning a corner at constant speed accelerating?

questions.q: Change in velocity divided by time is ___.
why: $a = \frac{\Delta v}{t}$
So velocity change ÷ time = acceleration.
questions.tip: Distance ÷ time = speed. **Velocity** ÷ time = acceleration.

similar.q: Displacement divided by time is ___.

questions.q: A net force of 8 N acts on a 2 kg object. Its acceleration is:
why: $a = \frac{F_n}{m}$
$a = \frac{8\text{ N}}{2\text{ kg}} = 4\text{ m/s}^2$
questions.tip: Cover **a** in the triangle: F over m.

similar.q: What acceleration does a force of 200 N give a 40 kg mass?

questions.q: You push a car at rest with a force of 500 N. What force does the car exert on you?
why: Newton's third law: action = reaction.
The car pushes back with 500 N, in the opposite direction.
questions.tip: The reaction is always the same number as the action.

similar.q: You push a table with 60 N. What force does the table put on you?

questions.q: A bike moves at a constant speed of 4 m/s for 5 seconds. How far does it go?
why: Constant velocity: $s = v \times t$
$s = 4\text{ m/s} \times 5\text{ s} = 20\text{ m}$
questions.tip: Speed × time = distance. Check: m/s × s = m.

similar.q: A bike goes 4 m/s for 10 minutes. How far does it go?

questions.q: The combination of all the forces acting on an object is the ___.
why: The textbook defines the net force ($F_n$) as the combination of all forces on an object.
questions.tip: "Net" means "all together".

similar.q: If forces are unbalanced, is the net force zero?

questions.q: How can forces of 3 N and 4 N be combined to give (a) 7 N and (b) 1 N?
questions.answer: (a) Put them in the same direction: 3 N + 4 N = 7 N. (b) Put them in opposite directions: 4 N − 3 N = 1 N.
why: Same direction → add: 3 + 4 = 7 N.
Opposite directions → subtract: 4 − 3 = 1 N (in the direction of the 4 N force).
questions.tip: Adding gives the biggest; subtracting gives the smallest.

similar.q: What net force do 3 N and 4 N give at a right angle?

questions.q: Forces of 8 N and 15 N at a right angle give a net force of 17 N.
why: Right angle → Pythagoras: $F_n^2 = 8^2 + 15^2$
$F_n = \sqrt{289} = 17\text{ N}$
questions.tip: Square both, add, then take the square root.

similar.q: Two workers push a box with 800 N south and 600 N west. What is the size of the net force?

questions.q: A car has a velocity of 72 km/h. How far does it travel in 15 minutes?
why: Make the units match: 15 minutes = $\frac{15}{60} = \frac{1}{4}$ hour.
$s = v \times t = 72\text{ km/h} \times \frac{1}{4}\text{ h}$
$s = 18\text{ km}$
questions.tip: km/h × hours = km. Change minutes into hours first.

similar.q: A car goes at 60 km/h for 30 minutes. How far does it go?

questions.q: Zahra's car goes from 14 m/s to 26 m/s in 2 minutes. What is its acceleration in m/s²?
questions.tip: Time must be in **seconds** for m/s².

similar.q: A train goes from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 3 s. Find its acceleration.

questions.q: The engine of a car pulls with a force of 4000 N. The acceleration is 2 m/s². What is the mass of the car?
why: $m = \frac{F}{a}$
$m = \frac{4000\text{ N}}{2\text{ m/s}^2} = 2000\text{ kg}$
questions.tip: Cover **m** in the triangle: F over a.

similar.q: A force of 40 N gives an object 2 m/s². Find its mass.

units.title: The Structure of the Atom
units.intro: This unit is about the atom, the three main subatomic particles, and how the particles are arranged in the atom.

u3solar.title: An atom is like the solar system

u3solar_q.title: An atom is like the solar system (quiz)

cards.title: Divide and divide again
body: Activity 3.1: take aluminium foil, paper, wood and chalk.
Divide each one into two. Go on dividing as far as you can.
Can you go on dividing for ever by ordinary means? Think about it.

steps.text: Take a **copper wire**. It is shiny and reddish brown.
Grind it into **copper dust**. Each piece is still shiny and reddish brown. It still shows the properties of copper.
Divide again and again. At last you find the **smallest particle** that still shows the properties of copper: an **atom**.

cards.title: What is an atom?
body: An **atom** is the smallest particle of an element that shows the properties of the element.

cards.title: Where does the word come from?
body: The Greek philosopher **Democritus** (460 – 370 B.C.) was the first to say that matter is made of tiny particles.
He called them **"atomos"**. It is a Greek word. It means **something that cannot be divided**.
The English word **atom** comes from "atomos".

cards.title: Everything is made of atoms
body: Every substance is made from atoms.
- **Living things**: plants, animals and you.
- **Non-living things**: rocks, soil, water and air.

cards.title: No one has seen an atom
body: Atoms are so small that **no one has seen them**.
But we believe they exist. The idea of atoms explains the results of many experiments.

cards.title: The atomic model
body: Scientists built an **atomic model** from experiments and these ideas:
1. Atoms are very small **spheres**. They can be of different sizes.
2. Scientists once thought atoms could not be divided. Now we know atoms **can** be broken into smaller parts.
3. Sometimes atoms join together into pairs or larger groups called **molecules**.

cards.title: Size of an atom
body: The size of an atom is measured in **angstrom units** (Å).
About **14 000 000 000** hydrogen atoms in a line measure **1 metre**.

cards.title: Mass of an atom
body: Atoms are very small, so their mass is very small too.
Grams are not easy to use: the numbers are tiny decimals.
Scientists compare the mass of an atom with a chosen standard atom. The unit is the **atomic mass unit** (amu).
$1\text{ amu} = 1.66 \times 10^{-24}\text{ g}$

cards.title: Two small units
body: **Size** of atoms → **angstrom** (Å). 1 Å = $10^{-10}$ m.
**Mass** of atoms → **atomic mass unit** (amu). 1 amu = $1.66 \times 10^{-24}$ g.

cards.title: Memory trick: size and mass
body: **A**ngstrom measures **A**cross (size).
**amu** has **m** for **m**ass.

cards.q: "Atomos" is a Greek word. It means:
cards.why: Democritus used "atomos": something that cannot be divided.

cards.title: Particles inside the atom
body: Atoms are made of smaller particles: **subatomic particles**.
More than thirty are known today.
In Grade 8 you learn the three main ones: the **proton**, the **neutron** and the **electron**.

cards.title: Meet the three particles
body: Tap the dots. Compare their size, mass and charge.

cards.title: One at a time
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Proton
states.text: **Proton**: mass **1 amu**, a single **positive** charge (+1).

states.label: Neutron
states.text: **Neutron**: mass **1 amu**, **no** charge (0). Its name shows it: **neutr**al.

states.label: Electron
states.text: **Electron**: mass **1/1840 amu** (almost nothing), a single **negative** charge (−1). It is the lightest.

cards.title: What the table shows
body: 1. The proton and the neutron have the **same mass** (1 amu).
2. The proton is **positive**, the electron is **negative**, the neutron has **no charge**.
3. The electron has almost **negligible** mass.

cards.title: Memory trick: P-N-E
body: **P**roton = **P**ositive. **N**eutron = **N**eutral.
The electron is the tiny one: 1840 electrons weigh as much as one proton.

cards.title: Activity 3.2: heavy and light
body: Stick 12 marbles together and weigh them (m₁). They are like protons and neutrons.
Weigh 6 cotton balls (m₂). They are like electrons.
Compare m₁ and m₂.

cards.q: Which is the lightest subatomic particle?
cards.why: The electron has a mass of only 1/1840 amu.

lessons.title: The Arrangement of the Subatomic Particles in the Atom

cards.title: Two regions of the atom
body: The atom has **two regions**:
1. the **nucleus**,
2. the **atomic shell**.

cards.title: The nucleus
body: The **nucleus**:
1. is made of **protons and neutrons**,
2. is fixed at the **centre** of the atom,
3. is the **heavy** part of the atom,
4. is **positively** charged.

cards.title: Why is the nucleus heavy?
body: Protons and neutrons are the **heaviest** subatomic particles (1 amu each).
They are in the nucleus.
So the **mass of the atom** is concentrated in the nucleus.

cards.title: The atomic shell
body: The atomic shell has **energy levels** (electron shells).
The **electrons** are in the shells. They **revolve** around the nucleus.

cards.title: Like the solar system
body: The atom is very like the solar system.
The sun is at the centre of the solar system. The **nucleus** is at the centre of the atom.
Tap the dots to compare.

cards.title: Energy levels
body: Energy levels are named with letters **K, L, M, N…** or numbers **n = 1, 2, 3, 4…**
Up to **seven** energy levels are enough for all known elements. Tap the dots.

cards.title: How many electrons fit?
body: Each shell has a fixed capacity. Move the slider.

states.label: K (n = 1)
states.text: The **first** shell (nearest to the nucleus) holds a maximum of **2** electrons.

states.label: L (n = 2)
states.text: The **second** shell holds a maximum of **8** electrons.

states.label: M (n = 3)
states.text: The **third** shell holds a maximum of **18** electrons.

cards.title: Filling the shells: four rules
body: 1. Electrons fill the levels **closest to the nucleus first**: K, then L, and so on.
2. The **outermost** shell can hold at most **8** electrons. The first shell holds at most **2**.
3. A shell does **not** have to be full.
4. When a level has 8 electrons (not the first level), a **new** level starts. This reduces the repulsion of similar charges.

cards.title: M holds 18, but the outside holds 8
body: The M-shell can hold up to **18**.
But the **outermost** shell holds at most **8** (rule 2 and rule 4).
So argon (18 electrons) is **2, 8, 8**, not 2, 16.

cards.title: 2, then 8, then the rest
body: Fill **K** first: up to **2**.
Then **L**: up to **8**.
Then the next shell gets the rest.
Always check: the numbers must add up to the number of electrons.

cards.title: Chlorine: 17 electrons

steps.text: Two electrons go into the **K-shell**. 17 − 2 = 15 are left.
The **L-shell** takes a maximum of **8**. 15 − 8 = 7 are left.
The last **7** go into the **M-shell**. Chlorine is **2, 8, 7**.

body: Tap Next to fill the shells one by one.

cards.title: Build an atom
body: Move the slider to see different atoms.

states.label: Helium
states.text: Helium: **2** electrons → **2**. Only the K-shell.

states.label: Carbon
states.text: Carbon: 6 electrons → **2, 4**.

states.label: Oxygen
states.text: Oxygen: 8 electrons → **2, 6**. The L-shell is not full, and that is fine.

states.label: Neon
states.text: Neon: 10 electrons → **2, 8**.

states.label: Sodium
states.text: Sodium: 11 electrons → **2, 8, 1**.

states.label: Chlorine
states.text: Chlorine: 17 electrons → **2, 8, 7**.

cards.title: Electronic configuration
body: Drawing atoms takes time. We can use a **shorthand**.
It is called the **electronic configuration** (electronic structure).
It shows the number of electrons in each shell, from the nucleus outwards.
Examples: helium **2**, carbon **2, 4**, sodium **2, 8, 1**.

cards.title: Count the electrons
body: Add the numbers to find the electrons:
- helium 2 → **2** electrons
- carbon 2, 4 → 2 + 4 = **6** electrons
- sodium 2, 8, 1 → 2 + 8 + 1 = **11** electrons

cards.title: Example: phosphorus
body: A phosphorus atom has **15 electrons**, 15 protons and 16 neutrons.
K: 2. Then L: 8. That is 10. The last 5 go to M.
Phosphorus is **2, 8, 5**. It has **3** energy levels.
15 protons (+15) and 15 electrons (−15): the charges cancel.

cards.title: Did you know? A 'person recipe'
head: Amount in a 50 kg person
Element
body: Our body is made of **10 different elements**.

cards.q: An atom has the electronic structure 2, 8, 3. How many electrons does it have?
cards.why: Add the shells: 2 + 8 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: All matter is composed of:
why: Every substance is made from atoms: living and non-living things.
questions.tip: The smallest building block of all matter is the **atom**.

similar.q: Are rocks and air made of atoms?
similar.a: Yes. All non-living things are made of atoms.

questions.q: Which statement is true?

options.D: Electrons are found in the nucleus.

why: The nucleus has protons (+) and neutrons (0). So it is positive.
Protons are in the nucleus, not the shell. Electrons are in the shells.
questions.tip: Nucleus = protons + neutrons = **positive**.

similar.q: What charge does a neutron have?

questions.q: The electronic structure of atom X is 2, 8, 3. How many electrons does X have?
why: Add the electrons in all shells.
questions.tip: Configuration → add. Number of electrons → split into 2, 8, …

similar.q: How many electrons does 2, 8, 7 show?

questions.q: Which statement is true?

options.A: All energy levels hold the same number of electrons.
options.B: The nucleus revolves around the energy levels.
options.C: A proton is positive because it has extra electrons.
options.D: The mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus.

why: The heaviest particles (protons and neutrons) are in the nucleus.
So most of the mass is in the nucleus.
A is wrong (2, 8, 18). B is wrong (electrons revolve, the nucleus is fixed).
questions.tip: Heavy particles → nucleus → mass of the atom.

similar.q: Why is the mass of an atom in the nucleus?
similar.a: Because the heaviest particles, protons and neutrons, are in the nucleus.

questions.q: The smallest particle of an element which shows the properties of the element is the ___.
why: This is the textbook definition of an **atom**.
questions.tip: Think of the copper dust: the smallest piece that is still copper is an atom.

similar.q: Atoms joined together in pairs or larger groups are called ___.

questions.q: The two regions of an atom are the nucleus and the ___.
why: The atom has two regions: the nucleus (centre) and the atomic shell (energy levels with electrons).
questions.tip: Centre + shells.

similar.q: Name the three main subatomic particles.

questions.q: The shell nearest to the nucleus can hold a maximum of ___ electrons.
why: K-shell (n = 1): maximum 2.
L-shell: 8. M-shell: 18.
questions.tip: Remember **2 – 8 – 18**.

similar.q: The 2nd and 3rd shells can hold a maximum of ___ and ___ electrons.

questions.q: Which particle has a mass of 1 amu and no charge?
why: Neutron: 1 amu, charge 0.
Proton: 1 amu, +1. Electron: 1/1840 amu, −1.
questions.tip: **Neutr**on = **neutr**al.

similar.q: Which particle is the basic unit of positive charge?

questions.q: Write the electronic configuration of (a) nitrogen, 7 electrons, (b) argon, 18 electrons, (c) aluminium, 13 electrons.
why: Nitrogen: K takes 2, 7 − 2 = 5 go to L → 2, 5.
Aluminium: K 2, L 8, 13 − 10 = 3 go to M → 2, 8, 3.
questions.tip: Subtract step by step: take 2, then 8, then write what is left.

similar.q: Write the configuration of phosphorus (15 electrons).

questions.q: In an oxygen atom (2, 6), the L-shell is full.
why: The L-shell can hold a maximum of 8.
Oxygen has only 6 in the L-shell.
A shell does not have to be full.
questions.tip: Compare with the maximum: 6 is less than 8.

similar.q: True or false: in neon (2, 8), the L-shell is full.

questions.q: What units do scientists use for (a) the size of atoms and (b) the mass of atoms?
why: Mass: 1 amu = $1.66 \times 10^{-24}$ g.
questions.tip: Å for length, amu for mass.

similar.q: How many hydrogen atoms in a line measure 1 metre?

questions.q: The second shell can hold ___ electrons.
why: The second shell holds a **maximum** of 8.
A shell can hold any number from 1 up to its maximum.
So 2 and 6 are both possible. 9 is too many.
questions.tip: When 8 is not an option, think: which numbers are **not more than 8**?

similar.q: Can the first shell hold 3 electrons?

questions.q: Phosphorus has 15 electrons. How many energy levels does it use? Write its shorthand.
why: K: 2 (13 left).
L: 8 (5 left).
Three shells are used: 2, 8, 5.
questions.tip: Count the numbers in the configuration: three numbers = three energy levels.

similar.q: How many energy levels does sodium (2, 8, 1) use?

units.title: Introduction to Chemical Reactions and the Periodic Table
units.intro: This unit is about chemical symbols and formulas, chemical reactions and equations, and the periodic table: metals, metalloids and nonmetals.

u4evidence.title: Signs that a chemical reaction happens

cards.title: What is a chemical symbol?
body: Most elements have long names.
A **chemical symbol** is one letter or two letters that stand for the name of an element.

cards.title: Three rules for symbols
body: a. Every symbol of a natural element has **one or two** letters.
b. The **first** letter is always a **capital** letter.
c. The **second** letter (if there is one) is always a **small** letter.

cards.title: Four elements that start with C
body: Move the slider (Table 4.1).

states.label: Carbon
states.text: Carbon → **C**: the first letter of the name.

states.label: Calcium
states.text: Calcium → **Ca**: the first two letters, so it is not confused with carbon.

states.label: Cobalt
states.text: Cobalt → **Co**: the first two letters of the name.

states.label: Copper
states.text: Copper → **Cu**: from its Latin name **cuprum**, so it is not confused with cobalt.

cards.title: Names from Latin
body: Most symbols come from the **English** name. A few come from the **Latin** name.

cards.title: Memory trick: the Latin six
body: **Au** sounds like "Ow!" – gold is expensive!
**Na**trium → **Na** → sodium. **Fe**rrum → **Fe** → iron.

cards.title: What is a chemical formula?
body: A **chemical formula** is a shorthand for the chemical composition of a compound.
It shows:
- which **elements** are present,
- the **ratio** of their atoms.

cards.title: Count the atoms
body: Move the slider to see some formulas from Table 4.3.

states.label: H₂O
states.text: **Water**: 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

states.label: CO₂
states.text: **Carbon dioxide**: 1 carbon atom with 2 oxygen atoms.

states.label: NaCl
states.text: **Sodium chloride**: 1 sodium atom with 1 chlorine atom.

states.label: Ca(OH)₂
states.text: **Calcium hydroxide**: 1 calcium atom, 2 oxygen atoms and 2 hydrogen atoms.

states.label: H₂SO₄
states.text: **Sulphuric acid**: 2 hydrogen atoms, 1 sulphur atom and 4 oxygen atoms.

cards.title: Numbers in a formula
body: The small number at the **bottom right** of a symbol is a **subscript**.
It tells the number of atoms of that element.
In H₂O, the 2 means **two** hydrogen atoms. There is **one** oxygen atom.
The number 1 is **never written**. The symbol alone means one atom.

cards.title: Brackets in a formula
body: Brackets show **groups** of atoms. The number after the bracket multiplies the whole group.
Ca(OH)₂ = 1 Ca + **2 groups of OH** = 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H.
(NH₄)₂SO₄ = 2 groups of NH₄ + 1 S + 4 O = **2 N, 8 H, 1 S, 4 O**.

cards.title: Read a formula in 3 steps
body: 1. Find each **capital** letter: each one starts a new element.
2. Read the small number after it (no number = 1).
3. A number after a **bracket** multiplies everything inside.

cards.title: Example: iron rust
body: The formula of iron rust is **Fe₂O₃** (Exercise 4.1).
It is made of **iron** and **oxygen**.
It has **2 iron atoms** and **3 oxygen atoms**.

cards.q: How many atoms of oxygen are in H₂SO₄?
cards.why: The 4 after O means four oxygen atoms.

cards.title: What is a chemical reaction?
body: A **chemical reaction** is a change in which one or more substances become **new substances**.
Atoms and molecules **rearrange** themselves to form new compounds.

cards.title: Examples
body: - **Magnesium** burns with oxygen with a brilliant white flame. It leaves a white ash.
- **Green plants** use carbon dioxide and water with sunlight to make food (carbohydrate) and oxygen.
- Cars burn **petrol**. Fuel gas burns in cookers.
- **Iron rusts**. Food is **digested** inside us.

cards.title: Three common characteristics
body: 1. They cause a **change of appearance** (colour). Example: hydrogen and oxygen, two colourless gases, make liquid water.
2. They are **difficult to reverse** or cannot be reversed. Example: it is very hard to turn brown iron rust back into grey iron.
3. They involve **energy changes**: heat, sound, light, mechanical or electrical energy.

cards.title: Energy from reactions
body: - **Fuels** give out heat and light.
- **Explosives** give a blast with mechanical and sound energy.
- A **battery** in a torch or radio has a chemical reaction that gives **electricity**.

cards.title: Memory trick: C-R-E
body: Chemical reactions **C.R.E.**ate new substances: **C**olour, **R**everse, **E**nergy.

cards.title: How do we know a reaction happened?
body: Figure 4.1 shows five signs. Tap the dots.

cards.title: What is a chemical equation?
body: A **chemical equation** is a shorthand that shows the changes in a chemical reaction.
It shows the starting substances, the **reactants**, and the new substances, the **products**.

cards.title: Build an equation

steps.text: Start with the **reactants**: carbon and oxygen.
The **arrow** means "yields" or "produces".
The **product** is carbon dioxide.

body: Charcoal (carbon) burns in air.

cards.title: Word equations
body: An equation written with words is a **word equation**.
Carbon + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide
Calcium carbonate $\xrightarrow{\text{heat}}$ Calcium oxide + Carbon dioxide
The second one is a **decomposition**: heat breaks calcium carbonate down.

cards.title: Equations with state symbols
body: $\text{CaCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$
$\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)$
CaCO₃, CaO and Ca(OH)₂ are solids. Water is a liquid. CO₂ is a gas that is given off.

cards.title: Left and right
body: **Left** of the arrow → **reactants** (what you start with).
**Right** of the arrow → **products** (what is made).
(aq) = **aq**ua = dissolved in water.

cards.q: In the reaction H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, which statement is true?
cards.why: H₂O is on the right of the arrow, so it is the product. H₂ and O₂ are both reactants.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Periodic Table of Elements

cards.title: Activity 4.1: sort 20 cards
body: Write the symbol and electronic structure of the first 20 elements on cards.
Try to put them into groups. What is the basis of your groups?

cards.title: What is the periodic table?
body: The **periodic table** is a way of **classifying** the chemical elements.
It is a very important tool for the **systematic study** of the properties of elements.

cards.title: How it is made
body: 1. Each element has a **box**. The box has information about the element. You only need the **symbol**.
2. The boxes make a grid of **periods** (horizontal **rows**) and **groups** (vertical **columns**).

cards.title: Explore the table
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Period
states.text: A **period** is a horizontal row.

states.label: Group
states.text: A **group** is a vertical column.

states.label: Metals
states.text: **Metals**: the large lower-left part. About **80 %** of the elements are metals.

states.label: Metalloids
states.text: **Metalloids** (semimetals): along the zigzag line, e.g. **silicon**.

states.label: Nonmetals
states.text: **Nonmetals**: the small upper-right part.

cards.title: Two patterns
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Across a period
states.text: From **left to right**: metals → metalloids → nonmetals. Left end = metals, right end = nonmetals.

states.label: Down a group
states.text: Going **down** a group, atoms get **bigger**. Each step down adds **one energy level**.

cards.title: Metals
body: - Generally **shiny solids** at room temperature. **Mercury** is the only liquid metal.
- **Conduct** heat and electricity well.
- **Malleable**: can be hammered into sheets.
- **Ductile**: can be drawn into wires.

cards.title: Nonmetals and metalloids
body: **Nonmetals** are generally gases, or dull, brittle solids. **Bromine** is the only liquid nonmetal. They are poor conductors of heat and electricity.
**Metalloids** (semimetals) have properties **between** metals and nonmetals. Example: **silicon**.

**Bromine**: the only liquid **nonmetal**.
**Graphite** (carbon) is a nonmetal that conducts electricity.

cards.title: Why we use metals
body: Move the slider to see how properties are used.

states.label: Hard
states.text: Most metals are **hard, strong and tough**. We make tools like **hammers**, screwdrivers and machines.

states.label: Malleable
states.text: Metals are **malleable**: they can be bent or hammered into **thin sheets**.

states.label: Ductile
states.text: Metals are **ductile**: they can be drawn into **thin wires**.

states.label: Conductor
states.text: Metals **conduct electricity**: electric wires, lamps, TV sets, calculators, fans.

states.label: High melting
states.text: Metals have **high melting and boiling points**. They do not melt easily when heated.

options.C: A symbol always uses the first and second letters of the name.
