units.title: Heat and Temperature
units.intro: This unit is about heat and its sources, how heat travels, surfaces and heat, expansion, temperature and its scales, specific heat, and which way heat travels.

u5sand.title: Sand and water at the beach

cards.title: Activity 5.1: hit and bend
body: Hit a steel rod with a hammer for a minute. Touch the rod.
Bend a wire back and forth until it breaks. Touch the broken end.
Both get **warm**. The energy you used becomes heat.

cards.title: Molecules are always moving
body: Matter is made of atoms. Atoms join to make **molecules**.
The molecules in a substance always **vibrate**: they move forward and backward very fast.

cards.title: Slow or fast?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Cool
states.text: The molecules vibrate **slowly**. There is less heat energy.

states.label: Hot
states.text: Hit a nail with a hammer. More energy of motion goes into the nail. Its molecules move **faster**. The faster they move, the **warmer** the nail.

cards.title: What is heat?
body: **Heat** is the energy of motion in the molecules of a substance.
If the vibration increases, the heat energy increases.

cards.title: Uses of heat
body: At home we use heat to **cook** food, **warm** our homes and **iron** clothes.
In industries, heat is used to **run machines**.

cards.title: Heat = moving molecules
body: More motion → more heat.
Less motion → less heat.
Heat moves from a **warmer** object to a **cooler** one.

cards.q: What do we call the energy of motion in the molecules of a substance?
cards.why: Heat is the energy of motion in the molecules of a substance.

cards.title: Many sources of heat
body: The **sun** is the **main** source of heat.
Heat also comes from **fuels**: coal, petrol, kerosene and natural gas.

cards.title: Four sources
body: Tap the dots (Figure 5.1).

cards.title: Electricity and friction
body: **Electric current** gives heat when it passes through bulbs, electric irons and heaters.
**Friction** happens when two surfaces rub against each other. One effect of friction is **heat**.

cards.title: Heat comes from other energy
body: Usually heat comes from **other forms of energy**.
Rub your hands together. You use **mechanical energy**. Your hands get warm: mechanical energy becomes heat.

cards.title: Memory trick: S-F-E-F
body: **S**ome **F**ires **E**at **F**ood: Sun, Fuels, Electricity, Friction.

cards.q: You rub your hands and they get warm. Which energy becomes heat?
cards.why: Rubbing uses mechanical energy. It is converted to heat.

cards.title: Heat moves from hot to cool
body: Heat always moves from a **hot** object to a **cool** object.
It moves in **three ways**: **conduction**, **convection** and **radiation**.

cards.title: A nail and a candle
body: Activity 5.3. Move the slider.

states.label: Nail in the flame
states.text: Put one end of a nail in the flame. The other end gets hot: **conduction**.

states.label: Hand above
states.text: Hold your hand above the flame. Hot air rises to your hand: **convection**.

states.label: Hand at the side
states.text: Hold your hand at the side. You still feel heat: **radiation**.

cards.title: Conduction along a rod

steps.text: Fix five pins on a metal rod with wax. Heat one end.
The wax near the flame melts first. The first pin falls.
Heat travels along the rod. The second pin falls.
Then the third pin…
…and the fourth.
At last the pin at the far end falls. Heat has travelled along the whole rod.

body: Activity 5.4. Tap Next.

cards.title: How conduction works
body: Heated molecules vibrate **faster**. They **collide** with their neighbours and pass on energy.
**Conduction** is heat transfer along vibrating and colliding molecules.
The molecules themselves do **not** move from one end to the other.
Conduction happens in solids, liquids and gases.

cards.title: Conductors and insulators
body: **Good conductors** conduct heat well: metals like **silver, copper, aluminium, iron**.
**Insulators** (bad conductors) conduct heat poorly: **wood, cork, wool, plastics**. Water and air are also poor conductors.

cards.title: Uses
body: Pots and pans are made of copper, aluminium or stainless steel. Heat travels easily through them to the food.
Their **handles** are made of insulators like **plastic** and **wood**.

cards.title: Convection in water

steps.text: Heat one side of a flask of water with sawdust. The warm water becomes **less dense** and **rises**.
The cool water goes down to take its place.
This goes round and round: a **convection current**. The sawdust shows the path.

body: Activity 5.5 A. Tap Next.

cards.title: What is convection?
body: **Convection** is heat transfer by **currents** of liquids and gases.
The warm liquid rises, the cool liquid sinks, until all the liquid is hot.
In convection the molecules **actually move**.
It happens in **liquids and gases**, but **not** in solids.

cards.title: Chimneys
body: Smoke and gases from fires rise up through **chimneys**.
This flow is due to **convection currents**.

cards.title: Sea breeze and land breeze
body: Convection makes gentle winds at coasts and lake shores. Move the slider.

states.label: Day
states.text: By **day** the land gets warmer than the sea. Warm air rises over the land. Cool air from the sea flows to the land: a **sea breeze**.

states.label: Night
states.text: At **night** the land cools faster than the sea. Cool air from the land flows to the sea: a **land breeze**.

cards.title: Breeze names
body: The breeze is named after **where it comes from**.
**Sea** breeze: from the sea, by day.
**Land** breeze: from the land, at night.

cards.title: What is radiation?
body: Conduction and convection need a **substance**.
But heat can also pass through **empty space** (a vacuum).
**Radiation** is heat transfer through a vacuum or empty space.

cards.title: Radiant energy
body: Every heated object, like a lighted bulb, sends out **radiant energy**.
Any object hotter than its surroundings radiates heat. **Light** is one form of radiant energy.
The sun's heat crosses empty space. So it reaches us by **radiation**, not by conduction or convection.

cards.title: The thermos flask
body: A **thermos** (vacuum) flask is a double-walled glass container. Tap the dots.

cards.title: How a thermos flask stops heat
head: Part
Stops heat moving by
rows: conduction, and convection of hot air above the liquid

cards.title: Uses of the flask
body: A thermos flask keeps hot drinks like tea, coffee and soup **hot**.
It also keeps cold drinks **cold** for a long time.

cards.title: Memory trick: Touch, Flow, Shine
body: Con**duc**tion → a **duc**k line: passed along, one to the next.
Con**vec**tion → hot air **goes up**.
**R**adiation → **R**ays from the sun.

cards.q: How does heat from the sun reach the earth?
cards.why: Space is empty (a vacuum). Only radiation can cross empty space.

cards.title: Why white clothes?
body: People in hot places like **white** clothes and paint their houses **white**. Why?
The answer is about how surfaces **radiate**, **reflect** and **absorb** heat.

cards.title: Black or shiny?
body: Activities 5.7 and 5.8. Move the slider.

states.label: Radiating
states.text: **Black** surfaces **radiate** (send out) heat better than shiny and white surfaces.

states.label: Absorbing
states.text: **Black** surfaces **absorb** heat better. **White and shiny** surfaces **reflect** heat better.

cards.title: Rough and smooth
body: **Rough** surfaces radiate heat better than smooth surfaces.
Rough surfaces are **good absorbers**. Smooth surfaces are **bad absorbers**.

cards.title: Good radiator = good absorber
body: Black and rough: **good** radiators and **good** absorbers.
White, shiny and smooth: **bad** radiators and **bad** absorbers, but **good reflectors**.

cards.title: Back to the flask
body: The silver walls of a vacuum flask are **shiny**. They reduce heat transfer by **radiation**.
The vacuum reduces transfer by **conduction** and **convection**.

cards.q: Dull black surfaces are ___ absorbers of heat.
cards.why: Black surfaces are better absorbers of heat than white or shiny ones.

cards.title: Ball and ring
body: Activity 5.9. Move the slider.

states.label: Cold ball
states.text: The cold metal ball **passes** through the ring easily.

states.label: Heated ball
states.text: Heat the ball for 15 minutes. Now it is **bigger**. It does **not** pass through the ring.

states.label: Cooled again
states.text: Let it cool for 10 minutes. It gets smaller and **passes** through again.

cards.title: Why things expand
body: Move the slider. Look at the space between the molecules.

states.label: Cool
states.text: The molecules are close together.

states.label: Heated
states.text: The molecules vibrate faster and **move away** from each other. There is more distance between them. The object **expands**.

cards.title: Expansion and contraction
body: **Expansion** is the increase in size of an object when it is **heated**. It takes up more space.
**Contraction** is the decrease in size of an object when it is **cooled**. It takes up less space.

cards.title: Liquids and gases too
body: Activity 5.10: coloured water in a tube in hot water **rises**. In cold water it **falls**.
Activity 5.11: a balloon on a bottle in hot water **blows up**. In cold water it goes **flat**.
Solids, liquids and gases all expand when heated and contract when cooled.

cards.title: Who expands most?
body: They expand at different rates.
On heating: **gases** expand more than **liquids**, and liquids more than **solids**.
On cooling: gases contract most, solids least.

cards.title: Memory trick: G > L > S
body: **G**ood **L**ittle **S**tudents: Gases > Liquids > Solids.

cards.title: Gaps in railway lines
body: Builders leave space for materials to expand. Move the slider.

states.label: Cold
states.text: In cold weather the metal contracts. The gap between the rails is **wide**.

states.label: Hot
states.text: In summer the metal expands. The gap gets **smaller**. The gap gives room to expand.

states.label: No gap
states.text: If no gap is left, the rails **bend** and are damaged on hot days.

cards.title: More examples
body: Small gaps are left in **concrete pavements**.
Space is left in **bridges** and **large buildings**.
Telephone and electric **wires** are put up slightly **loose** in warm weather. Then in cold weather they can contract without breaking.

cards.q: What happens to most materials when they get warmer?
cards.why: Solids, liquids and gases normally expand when heated.

cards.title: Activity 5.12: three dishes
body: Put one hand in cold water and one in hot water. After 3 minutes put both hands in warm water.
The hands feel **different** in the same water! Touch gives only a **rough** measure of hotness.

cards.title: What is temperature?
body: **Temperature** is a measure of the degree of **hotness or coldness** of an object.
Heat and temperature are **not** the same. Heat, like light, is a form of **energy**.

cards.title: The thermometer
body: A **thermometer** measures temperature accurately.
A common type is a glass tube with **mercury** or **coloured alcohol**.
The liquid expands when the temperature rises and contracts when it falls.

cards.title: Making a scale
body: A scale needs **two fixed points**:
- **lower fixed point**: pure water **freezes**,
- **upper fixed point**: pure water **boils** (normal atmospheric pressure).
The space between them is divided into equal parts called **degrees**.

cards.title: Celsius and Fahrenheit
body: Move the slider. Compare the two scales.

states.label: Water freezes
states.text: Pure water freezes at **0 °C** = **32 °F**.

states.label: Body
states.text: Normal body temperature: **37 °C** = **98.6 °F**.

states.label: Water boils
states.text: Pure water boils at **100 °C** = **212 °F**.

cards.title: Converting
body: Celsius to Fahrenheit:
Fahrenheit to Celsius:

cards.title: Worked example: body temperature
body: $T_C = 37$ °C. Find $T_F$.

cards.title: Worked example: hot day
body: $T_F = 86$ °F. Find $T_C$.

cards.title: Order matters
body: **C → F**: multiply by $\frac{9}{5}$ **first**, then **add** 32.
**F → C**: **subtract** 32 **first**, then multiply by $\frac{5}{9}$.

cards.title: Clinical thermometer
body: Clinics use a special **clinical thermometer**.
To read it: hold the **stem**. Keep your eyes **level** with the top of the liquid. Read the nearest mark (Figure 5.18).

cards.title: Fever
body: Normal body temperature is **37 °C**.
A child with more than **38 °C** has a **high fever** and is sick.
With a high temperature, go to the nearest clinic for treatment.

cards.q: Pure water boils at:
cards.why: On the Celsius scale water boils at 100 °C (212 °F).

cards.title: Grass and pavement
body: On a hot day you can walk barefoot on grass. But asphalt or sand on a street is very hot. Why?
The answer is **specific heat**.

cards.title: Units of heat
body: A **calorie** is the heat needed to raise the temperature of **1 gram of water** by **1 °C**.
Today we use the **joule** (J). It is the **SI unit** of heat.
1 calorie ≈ **4.2 joules**.

cards.title: What is specific heat?
body: The **specific heat** of a substance is the heat needed to raise the temperature of **1 kg** of it by **1 °C**.
Different substances have **different** specific heats.

cards.title: At the beach
body: Sand has a **lower** specific heat than water. Move the slider.

states.label: Hot day
states.text: The sand heats up **faster** than the water. The sand feels much warmer.

states.label: Night
states.text: At night the sand feels **cool** and the water feels **warmer**.

cards.title: Low specific heat = quick change
body: A **low** specific heat means it heats up **fast** (and cools fast).
Sand: low. Water: higher.
Same heat to equal masses? The one with the **lowest** specific heat gets **hottest**.

cards.title: Activity 5.14
body: Put 500 g of sand and 500 g of water in the sun for an hour. Which gets hotter?
Then put them in the shade. Which cools more quickly?

cards.title: Memory trick: cal and kg
body: **C**alorie is **s**mall: 1 **g**ram of water.
**S**pecific heat is for a **big** 1 **kg** of any substance.

cards.q: One calorie is about:
cards.why: The textbook says 1 cal is about 4.2 J.

cards.title: Why does tea get cold?
body: A cup of hot tea on a table becomes cool. A hot iron slowly cools. Where does the heat go?

cards.title: Mixing hot and cold

steps.text: Beaker A has **hot** water. Beaker B has **cold** water.
Mix them. Heat moves from the **hot** water to the **cold** water.
Heat stops moving when both reach the **same temperature**.

body: Activity 5.15. Tap Next.

cards.title: The rule
body: Heat always travels from **higher** temperature to **lower** temperature.
It goes on until both substances reach the **same temperature**.

cards.title: Heat lost = heat gained
body: When hot and cold substances are mixed, the hot one **loses** heat. The cold one **gains** the same amount.
Example: hot milk mixed with cold water.
**Heat lost by hot milk = heat gained by cold water**

cards.title: Hot gives, cold takes
body: Heat goes **from hot to cold**, never the other way by itself.
A hot nail in cold water: heat goes from the **nail** to the **water**.

cards.q: When heat travels between two objects, it moves to:
cards.why: Heat always travels from higher temperature to lower temperature.

tips.text: Three ways of heat transfer: **conduction** (solids, touching), **convection** (liquids and gases, currents), **radiation** (empty space).
Thermos flask questions: vacuum → conduction and convection; shiny walls → radiation; cork → conduction (and convection).
Black and rough = good radiator and good absorber. White and shiny = good reflector.

questions.q: A person standing in front of a fireplace is warmed mostly by:
why: The person is at the **side** of the fire, not above it and not touching it.

questions.q: Which is true?

options.A: Warm air is less dense than cool air.
options.B: Warm air is as dense as cool air.
options.D: Warm air is denser than cool air.

why: A heated liquid or gas becomes less dense, so it rises.
That is why warm air rises over the land by day.
questions.tip: Warm rises because it is lighter (less dense).

similar.q: In a flask heated from below, does warm water rise or sink?

questions.q: The temperature of an object is a measure of:

options.C: how hot or cold the object is

why: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of an object.
questions.tip: Temperature → how hot. Heat → energy.

similar.q: What instrument measures temperature?

questions.q: The same amount of heat is added to equal masses of four objects. Which becomes hottest?
why: Specific heat is the heat needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C.
Low specific heat → little heat needed per degree → the temperature rises most.
Like sand, which heats up faster than water.
questions.tip: Low specific heat = heats up fast.

similar.q: Which heats up faster in the sun, sand or water?

questions.q: When heat travels between two objects, it moves:
why: Heat always travels from higher temperature to lower temperature.
questions.tip: Hot gives, cold takes.

similar.q: A hot nail is dropped in cold water. Heat travels from ___ to ___.
similar.a: from the nail to the water

questions.q: All metals are good conductors. Plastics, water and air are bad conductors, or good ___.
why: Substances that conduct heat poorly are called bad conductors or insulators.
questions.tip: Handles are made of insulators.

similar.q: Heat energy can travel through empty space by ___.

questions.q: A patient's temperature is 104 °F. What is it in °C?
questions.tip: Subtract 32 first. 72 ÷ 9 = 8, then × 5.

similar.q: A thermometer reads 122 °F. What is the Celsius reading?

questions.q: Convert 75 °C to Fahrenheit.

similar.q: Your temperature is 38 °C. What is it in °F?

questions.q: Normal human body temperature is 98.6 °F or ___ °C.
why: The textbook: normal body temperature is 37 °C.
questions.tip: Above 38 °C is a high fever.

similar.q: Is 39 °C a normal body temperature?
similar.a: No. Over 38 °C is a high fever.

questions.q: When an object is heated, its molecules move closer together.
why: Heated molecules vibrate faster and move **away** from each other.
So the object expands.
questions.tip: Heat → faster → farther apart → bigger.

similar.q: What is the decrease in size of an object when cooled called?

questions.q: Hot drinks are kept warm in a vacuum flask. Why are the walls silvery, and why is there a vacuum?
questions.answer: The shiny silvery walls stop heat loss by radiation. The vacuum stops heat loss by conduction and convection.
why: Shiny surfaces are poor radiators and good reflectors.
Conduction and convection need a substance; a vacuum has none.
questions.tip: Two parts: silver → radiation; vacuum → conduction and convection.

similar.q: Why is the lid (cork) kept tightly closed?
similar.a: The cork is a good insulator. It stops heat loss by conduction and stops convection of hot air above the liquid.

questions.q: Explain why a sea breeze blows during the day.
questions.answer: By day the land gets warmer than the sea. Warm air rises over the land, and cooler air from the sea flows in to the land.
why: Land heats up faster than the sea by day.
Warm air over the land rises (convection).
Cool air from the sea moves in to take its place: a sea breeze.
questions.tip: Name the breeze after where the air comes **from**.

similar.q: Which breeze blows at night?
similar.a: the land breeze (from the land to the sea)

questions.q: List from coldest to warmest: 50 °C, 80 °F.
why: Change 80 °F to Celsius: $\frac{5}{9}(80 - 32) = \frac{5}{9} \times 48 \approx 26.7$ °C.
26.7 °C is colder than 50 °C.
questions.tip: Put both on the same scale first.

similar.q: Which is hotter: 30 °C or 80 °F?

units.title: Inheritance
units.intro: This unit is about genes and chromosomes, cell division, Mendel's genetic crosses, sources of variation, and inherited and acquired traits.

u6beads.title: Genes on chromosomes, like beads on a string

u6beads_q.title: Genes on chromosomes, like beads on a string (quiz)

cards.title: What is a gene?
body: A **gene** is the smallest part of a chromosome.
It decides one **trait** (feature) of an organism.
Different genes decide different traits.

cards.title: Beads on a string
body: Genes on a chromosome are arranged **one after the other**, like **beads on a string**.
Tap the dots.

cards.title: Genes come in pairs
body: In the nucleus of a **body cell**, chromosomes and genes come in **pairs**.
The two chromosomes of a pair are joined by a **centromere**.
The centromere is like a **button** that holds the two sides of a cloth.

cards.title: Two kinds of cell division
body: During cell division, chromosomes and genes **separate**.
There are two types of cell division: **mitosis** and **meiosis**.

cards.title: Mitosis

steps.text: One pair of chromosomes in the nucleus.
Each chromosome makes an **identical copy** of itself.
The cell starts to divide into **two**.
**Two** new daughter cells. Each has the **same number** of chromosomes as the parent cell.

body: Figure 6.1. Tap Next.

cards.title: Where does mitosis happen?
body: Mitosis happens only in **body cells**: skin cells, blood cells, muscle cells and bone cells.
At the end, the parent cell and the new cells have the **same number** of chromosomes.

cards.title: Meiosis

steps.text: One pair of chromosomes in the nucleus.
Each chromosome makes an identical copy of itself.
The cell starts to divide into **four**.
**Four** sex cells (sperms or eggs). Each has a **single** chromosome: half the number.

body: Figure 6.2. Tap Next.

cards.title: Where does meiosis happen?
body: Meiosis happens only in:
- the **testes**, to make sperms,
- the **anthers**, to make pollen grains,
- the **ovaries**, to make ova (eggs).
The sex cells get **half** the chromosomes of the body cell. Their genes are **unpaired**.

cards.title: Human numbers
body: A human **body cell** has **two sets** of chromosomes.
A **sperm** or an **ovum** has **one set**.
Each set has **23** chromosomes.

cards.title: Memory trick: mi-TWO-sis?

letters.m: make eggs and sperm: 4 cells, half

body: **Mi**tosis → **Mi**rror copies (same number).
M**ei**osis → s**e**x cells (half).

cards.q: How many daughter cells does mitosis make?
cards.why: Mitosis makes two new daughter cells (Figure 6.1).

cards.title: What is genetics?
body: **Genetics** is the study of **inheritance**.
It studies how traits are passed on from generation to generation.

cards.title: Gregor Mendel
body: **Gregor Mendel** (1822–1884) did crossing (breeding) experiments on **pea plants**.
He studied **one trait at a time**. Examples: height (tall or short), seed colour (yellow or green).

cards.title: Homozygous and heterozygous
body: A pair of **similar** genes is **homozygous**: TT (tall) or tt (short).
A pair of **different** genes is **heterozygous**: Tt.

cards.title: Artificial cross pollination
body: A pea flower is **bisexual**.
Mendel dusted pollen from the **tall** plant onto the stigma of the **short** plant **by hand**. He also did it the other way.
This is **artificial cross pollination**. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Mendel's crosses
body: Move the slider.

states.label: P1
states.text: **P1**: homozygous **tall** (TT, 2.0 m) and homozygous **short** (tt, 0.3 m) pea plants.

states.label: F1
states.text: **F1**: plants from the seeds of P1. They have mixed genes (**heterozygous**) and are called **hybrids**. But they were **all tall**!

states.label: F2
states.text: Mendel let the F1 flowers **self pollinate**. The **F2** plants were **¾ tall and ¼ short**. The short trait came back.

cards.title: Monohybrid cross
body: Crossing **one trait at a time** is called a **monohybrid** genetic cross.

cards.title: Make the crossing table
body: Activities 6.3 and 6.4 ask you to make a table. Move the slider.

states.label: P1 → F1
states.text: Tall parent gives **T**, short parent gives **t**. Every box is **Tt**. So all F1 plants are **tall** hybrids.

states.label: F1 → F2
states.text: Each F1 parent gives **T** or **t**. Boxes: TT, Tt, Tt, tt. **3 tall** (1 TT + 2 Tt) and **1 short** (tt): ¾ tall, ¼ short.

cards.title: Hidden, then back
body: In F1 the short trait was **hidden**: all plants were tall.
A trait hidden in the F1 is called **recessive** (p. 146).
In F2 the short trait appeared again in ¼ of the plants.

cards.title: Remember the fractions
body: **F1**: all tall (Tt).
**F2**: ¾ tall, ¼ short.
In F2: 1 TT, 2 Tt, 1 tt.

cards.title: Memory trick: P, F1, F2
body: **P**arents, **F**irst children, then **F**amily grandchildren.

cards.q: The offspring of two homozygous parents (TT × tt) is the:
cards.why: Mendel crossed homozygous tall and short plants (P1). Their offspring are the F1.

cards.title: No two are the same
body: No two living things are completely identical.
The differences between them are called **variations**.

cards.title: Two ways variations arise
body: 1. They are **passed on** from parents to offspring in sexual reproduction, or
2. They are **caused by the environment** where the organism lives.

cards.title: From parents: genetic cross
body: At **fertilization**, the genes and chromosomes of the male and female gametes **mix**.
This mixing causes variation in the offspring.

cards.title: From parents: changed genes
body: Genes are **not always stable**.
During meiosis, some genes or chromosomes may **change**.
A change in genes or chromosomes causes a change in traits.

cards.title: Main sources of variation
body: In sexually reproducing organisms the main sources are:
- **genetic crosses** (mixing at fertilization),
- **changes** in genes or chromosomes.
These variations are passed on from generation to generation.

cards.title: From the environment
body: **Population density**, **food supply**, **diseases**, **light** and **climate** can change how an organism looks.

cards.title: Seedlings from the same plant
body: Seeds of the same plant grow differently in different places. Move the slider.

states.label: Dark
states.text: Planted in the **dark**.

states.label: Shadow
states.text: Planted **under shadow**.

states.label: Full sun
states.text: Planted in **full sunlight**.

cards.title: Genes or environment?
body: It depends on the trait.
- **Flower colour** is controlled almost completely by **genes**.
- **Adult body weight** is strongly influenced by the **environment**, like the fat or carbohydrate in food.
Variations caused by the environment are **not passed on** to the offspring.

cards.q: Which is an environmental condition that can cause variation?
cards.why: Population density, food supply, diseases, light and climate are environmental conditions.

cards.title: Inherited traits
body: Traits passed on from parents to offspring are **inherited traits**.
They pass from generation to generation.
They are controlled by **genes** inside chromosomes.

cards.title: Acquired traits
body: Traits caused by the **environment** are **acquired traits**.
They are **not** passed on to the offspring.
They are **not** controlled by genes.

cards.title: Inherited traits in people
body: Figures 6.7 and 6.8. Move the slider.

states.label: Tongue
states.text: Some people can **roll** their tongue. Some cannot.

states.label: Thumb
states.text: A **bent** thumb or a **straight** thumb.

states.label: Ear lobe
states.text: A **free** ear lobe or an **attached** ear lobe.

states.label: Clasping hands
states.text: Clasp your hands. **Left thumb on top** is **dominant**. **Right thumb on top** is **recessive**.

cards.title: Activity 6.6: clasp your hands
body: Clasp your hands with the fingers between each other. Which thumb is on top?
Try the other thumb on top. Which way feels more comfortable?
Ask your family too (Activity 6.7). Who has the same way as you?

cards.title: Examples from Activity 6.5
head: Inherited (from genes)
Acquired (from the environment)
rows: a tattoo on the gum or skin

cards.title: Ask: did I get it from my parents?
body: **Yes** → inherited (genes).
**No, it happened in my life** → acquired (environment).
Acquired traits are **never** passed on to children.

cards.title: Memory trick: I and A

letters.m: acquired: from the world around you

body: **I**nherited = **I**nside genes. **A**cquired = **A**round you.

cards.q: A scar on your arm from a fall is:
cards.why: A scar is caused by the environment (an accident). It is not controlled by genes.

thread in the nucleus that carries genes
a feature of an organism, e.g. height or colour

cell division in body cells: 2 cells, same number of chromosomes
cell division that makes sex cells with half the chromosomes
the study of inheritance
a pair of similar genes, e.g. TT or tt
a pair of different genes, e.g. Tt
an F1 offspring with mixed (heterozygous) genes
dusting pollen by hand onto the stigma of another plant
a genetic cross of one trait at a time
a trait hidden in the F1
the trait that shows, e.g. left thumb on top
a difference between living things

tips.text: Mitosis: **body** cells, **2** cells, **same** number. Meiosis: **sex** cells, **4** cells, **half**.
Human numbers: body cell = **2 sets**, sex cell = **1 set**, one set = **23** chromosomes.
Mendel: P1 (TT × tt) → F1 all tall (Tt) → F2 **¾ tall, ¼ short**.
Homozygous = two **same** letters (TT, tt). Heterozygous = two **different** letters (Tt).
Inherited or acquired? If it came from an accident, exercise or tattoo, it is **acquired**.
Main sources of variation: **genetic cross** at fertilization and **changes** in genes or chromosomes.

items.text: The offspring of the P1 generation are the ___ generation.
The F1 pea plants were all ___.
The F2 plants were ¾ tall and ___ short.
A pair of similar genes (TT) is ___.
Crossing one trait at a time is a ___ cross.

cards.back: Smallest part of a chromosome; decides a trait.
Joins a pair of chromosomes, like a button.

F1 offspring with mixed genes (Tt).
Differences between living things.

items.text: Genes are arranged like beads on a string.
Mitosis happens only in the testes and ovaries.
items.why: That is meiosis. Mitosis is in body cells.

items.text: A human sex cell has 23 chromosomes.
The F1 pea plants were all short.
items.why: They were all tall.

items.text: Variations from the environment are passed on to offspring.
items.why: They are not passed on.

items.text: Flower colour is controlled almost completely by genes.
Left thumb on top is dominant.
A tattoo is an inherited trait.
items.why: It is acquired.

questions.q: A pair of similar genes that represent a trait is called:
why: Homo- = same: TT or tt.
Hetero- = different: Tt.
questions.tip: **Homo** = the **same**.

similar.q: What are Tt genes called?

questions.q: The offspring of two homozygous parents is the:
why: P1 = the homozygous parents (TT and tt).
Their seeds grow into the F1.

similar.q: What are the offspring of the F1 called?

questions.q: Differences among members of the same family are called:
why: Differences between living things are variations.
questions.tip: Vary = be different.

similar.q: Name two ways variations arise.
similar.a: passed on from parents; caused by the environment

questions.q: Traits that are NOT passed on from generation to generation are:
why: Acquired traits are caused by the environment.
They are not controlled by genes, so they are not passed on.
questions.tip: Acquired = from life around you.

similar.q: Traits passed on from generation to generation are called ___ traits.

questions.q: Dusting pollen grains by hand on the stigma of a flower is:
why: Mendel dusted pollen by hand.
Doing it by hand (not by nature) is artificial (cross) pollination.
questions.tip: By hand = artificial.

similar.q: What did Mendel let the F1 flowers do?

questions.q: Homozygous yellow peas crossed with homozygous green peas gave only yellow seeds. These yellow seeds are called ___.
why: They are F1 offspring with mixed genes from both parents.
F1 offspring with heterozygous genes are hybrids.
questions.tip: F1 = hybrid.

similar.q: What are Mendel's F1 tall plants called?

questions.q: A genetic cross of only one trait is called a ___ cross.
why: Mono = one. Crossing one trait at a time is monohybrid.
questions.tip: **Mono** = one.

similar.q: What trait did Mendel study in the tall and short plants?

questions.q: At the end of mitosis, the new cells have half the number of chromosomes.
why: Mitosis keeps the **same** number.
Meiosis gives half.
questions.tip: Mitosis = mirror copy.

similar.q: How many sex cells does meiosis make in Figure 6.2?

questions.q: Is there a difference in the number of chromosomes of body cells and sex cells? Why?
questions.answer: Yes. A body cell has two sets (2 × 23), a sex cell has one set (23). Sex cells are made by meiosis, which halves the number.
why: Human body cell: two sets of 23.
Sperm or ovum: one set of 23.
Meiosis makes sex cells with half the chromosomes.
questions.tip: Say the numbers and name the division (meiosis).

similar.q: How many chromosomes are in one set?

questions.q: What are the main sources of variation in sexually reproducing organisms?
questions.answer: Genetic crosses (mixing of genes at fertilization) and changes in genes or chromosomes.
why: At fertilization male and female genes mix.
During meiosis genes or chromosomes may change.
questions.tip: Two answers: **mixing** and **changing**.

similar.q: Name three environmental conditions that cause variation.
similar.a: Any three: population density, food supply, diseases, light, climate.

questions.q: Acquired traits are not passed on from parents to offspring. Why?
questions.answer: Because they are caused by the environment and are not controlled by genes.
why: Only traits controlled by genes are passed on.
Acquired traits come from the environment.
questions.tip: Use the word **genes** in your answer.

similar.q: Why do offspring look like their parents?
similar.a: They inherit genes (on chromosomes) from both parents.

questions.q: Cross two F1 pea plants (Tt × Tt). What gene pairs appear in the F2, and how many are tall and short?
questions.answer: TT, Tt, Tt, tt: 3 tall and 1 short (¾ tall, ¼ short).
why: Each parent gives T or t.
Table: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
Any plant with T is tall: 3. tt is short: 1.
questions.tip: Draw the 2 × 2 table.

similar.q: How many F2 plants in the table are homozygous tall?

units.title: Space Travel
units.intro: This unit is about the layers of the atmosphere, rockets and gravity, satellites, and space exploration of the moon and Mars.

cards.title: What is the atmosphere?
body: **Air** is a mixture of different gases.
The earth's **atmosphere** is the air around the earth, like a **blanket**.
It goes from sea level up to about **1600 km**.

cards.title: Held by gravity
body: The earth's **gravity** holds the air in place.
The atmosphere gets **thinner** as you go higher.

cards.title: Four layers
body: Scientists divide the atmosphere into **four** layers. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Climb through the layers
body: Move the slider from the ground up.

states.label: Troposphere
states.text: **Troposphere**: the lowest layer, up to about **16 km** at the equator (8 km at the poles). We live here. It has more than **75 %** of the atmosphere. **Weather** happens here.

states.label: Stratosphere
states.text: **Stratosphere**: from about **16 km** to **50 km**. It has the **ozone layer**. Pilots like to fly here: little weather disturbance.

states.label: Mesosphere
states.text: **Mesosphere**: between **50 and 80 km**. Extremely **strong winds** blow here.

states.label: Thermosphere
states.text: **Thermosphere**: the **uppermost** layer. The air is extremely thin. Its lower part **reflects radio waves** back to the earth.

states.label: Space
states.text: Beyond the thermosphere is **space**: the region beyond the earth's atmosphere.

cards.title: The troposphere and weather
body: Winds, storms, clouds, rain, snow and other weather happen in the **troposphere**.
It is the most important layer for human activity.
Scientists **forecast the weather** by studying the troposphere.

cards.title: The ozone layer
body: The **ozone layer** protects life from **ultraviolet rays**: harmful rays from the sun.
Many scientists think **pollutants** make the ozone layer thinner.
Then more ultraviolet rays get through. This causes more **skin cancer**.

cards.title: The thermosphere
body: More than **99.99 %** of the atmosphere lies below it.
It is completely exposed to the sun's radiation.
The lower part is important for **radio communication**.
The upper part has so little air that spacecraft there meet almost **no resistance**.

cards.title: Memory trick: T-S-M-T
body: From the ground up: **Tall Snakes Move Twice**.

cards.q: Which layer plays an important part in radio communication?
cards.why: The lower thermosphere reflects radio waves back to the earth.

cards.title: A balloon rocket

steps.text: Blow up a balloon. Close it with a peg. Tape a straw to it and pass a tight string through the straw.
Take away the peg and let go. Air rushes out of the back. The balloon **shoots along the string** the other way.

body: Activity 7.2. Tap Next.

cards.title: What is a rocket?
body: A **rocket** is a space vehicle that is forced to travel through air and space.
Rockets are the **only** vehicles that can travel through space.
They fly **higher and faster** than airplanes.

cards.title: Uses of rockets
body: Scientists use rockets for:
- **space exploration**,
- **scientific study**,
- **war**, in the atmosphere and in space.
Rockets carry instruments to explore the **moon**, the **planets** and the space between the planets.

cards.title: What is gravity?
body: **Gravity** is a force that **every object** puts on **every other object**.
The earth's gravity keeps the **moon** going round the earth.
The moon's gravity pulls on the earth too. But it is not strong enough to move the earth in space.

cards.title: Why things fall back
body: Things thrown up come back down because of the earth's **gravity**.
Gravity reaches into space. It gets **weaker** as you go farther from the earth.

cards.title: How fast must a rocket go?
body: Rockets must be very powerful to move against gravity. Move the slider.

states.label: Thrown up
states.text: A ball thrown up slows down and **falls back** because of gravity.

states.label: Correct speed
states.text: A rocket launched at the **correct speed** goes into **orbit** round the earth.

states.label: About 11 km/s
states.text: Launched at a very high speed, about **11 km/s**, a rocket **escapes** the earth's gravity.

cards.title: Big numbers
body: Escape speed: about **11 km/s**.
That is 11 kilometres every second!

cards.title: Magnet and paper clip
body: In Activity 7.3 the magnet pulls a paper clip. When the clip is far away, the magnet cannot pull it.
Gravity is like this: it gets weaker far from the earth.

cards.q: The force that keeps the moon going round the earth is:
cards.why: The earth's gravity keeps the moon revolving around the earth.

cards.title: What is a satellite?
body: A **satellite** is an object that travels round another object in space.
There are two types: **natural** and **artificial** satellites.

cards.title: Natural or artificial?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Natural
states.text: **Natural satellites** are natural objects that go round other objects. The earth and planets go round the sun. The **moon** goes round the earth.

states.label: Artificial
states.text: **Artificial satellites** are **man-made**. They go round the earth or other bodies. Examples: **communication** and **military** satellites.

cards.title: Six types by mission
body: Artificial satellites are grouped by their **mission** (job). Tap the dots.

cards.title: What does each one do?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Research
states.text: **Scientific research** satellites gather information for scientific study.

states.label: Navigation
states.text: **Navigation** satellites help ships and airplanes know their exact **position**.

states.label: Weather
states.text: **Weather** satellites watch the atmosphere over large areas. They help to **forecast the weather**.

states.label: Communications
states.text: **Communications** satellites are **relay stations**. They receive radio signals and send them on. They link people by **telephone, television and computer**.

states.label: Earth observation
states.text: **Earth observation** satellites map the earth's resources. They find minerals and fresh water, find pollution, and see disease in crops and forests.

states.label: Military
states.text: **Military** ("spy") satellites watch military movements, detect missile launches and pick up communication between countries.

cards.title: Memory trick: six missions
body: **Some Nice Weather Can Easily Move.**

cards.title: Orbits
body: The path of a satellite is its **orbit**.
Orbits are at different heights: some about **250 km** above the earth, others more than **32 200 km**.

cards.title: What keeps a satellite up?
body: Activity 7.4: swing a container of water on a string. Move the slider.

states.label: Container on a string
states.text: The string pulls the container round in a circle. The water stays in.

states.label: Satellite
states.text: **Gravity** pulls the satellite round its path. It stays in orbit because of the **balance** between its **velocity** and the earth's **gravity**.

states.label: Different heights
states.text: Some orbits are about **250 km** high. Others are more than **32 200 km** high.

cards.q: Which satellites are often called 'spy satellites'?
cards.why: Military satellites are often called spy satellites.

cards.title: What is space like?
body: **Space** is the region beyond the earth's atmosphere, between all objects in the universe.
It is like a clear, dark night, but the sun, moon and stars shine all the time.
There is **no air** to breathe. This makes it hard for people to live in space.

cards.title: What is space exploration?
body: **Space exploration** is the mission to discover the nature of the universe beyond the earth.
Spacecraft go far beyond the earth to collect information.
It may show how the sun, planets and stars were formed, and whether life exists beyond our world.

cards.title: The space age

steps.text: **1957**: the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, the **first artificial satellite**. The space age began.
**1958**: the United States and the Soviet Union began to send **probes** to the moon and planets.
**1961**: **Yuri Gagarin** made the **first space flight**. He went once round the earth in **108 minutes**.
**1969**: two U.S. astronauts landed on the **moon** for the first time.
**1969 – 1972**: Apollo astronauts made **six** landings on the moon.
**2005**: the United States launched the spacecraft **Discovery**.

body: Tap Next to move through time.

cards.title: The space race
body: In the early space age the **United States** and the **Soviet Union** competed.
The West reacted to Sputnik with surprise, fear and respect.
Later the United States decided to send astronauts to the moon.

cards.title: Space probes
body: A **space probe** is an **unmanned** device sent to explore space.
It may go far out, go round a planet or moon, or land on it.
It may make a one-way trip or bring samples and data back.
It observes temperature, radiation and objects in space.

cards.title: Landing on the moon
body: On **20 July 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** and **Edwin Aldrin** landed **Apollo 11** on the moon.
Armstrong said: "That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."
They collected rocks and soil, set up equipment and took photographs.

cards.title: Exploring Mars
body: Sending people to **Mars** may be the next great adventure.
A round trip would take about **two years**. The spacecraft must carry fuel, food, supplies and living space.
Mars has an **atmosphere**, so it will be easier to approach than the moon.

cards.title: Mars and the earth
body: The earth's climate is **more like Mars** than any other planet.
If Mars had more air and were a little warmer, it would be much like the earth.
Studying Mars' climate might help predict climate changes on the earth.

cards.title: Firsts to remember
body: First artificial satellite: **Sputnik 1** (1957).
First person in space: **Yuri Gagarin** (1961).
First on the moon: **Neil Armstrong** (Apollo 11, 1969).

cards.title: Water is everywhere
body: Water comes from **different sources**.
Water covers nearly **three-quarters** of the earth's surface.
It is mainly in **oceans**, but also in rivers, lakes and glaciers, in the **atmosphere** and **underground**.

cards.title: Salty or fresh?
body: Look at the 100 squares. Move the slider.

states.label: Salty water
states.text: Over **97 %** of the earth's water is **salty**.

states.label: The rest
states.text: Only the **remainder** (the last few squares) is **freshwater**.

cards.title: What is freshwater?
body: **Freshwater** is water that has **less than 1000 milligrams** of dissolved solids (salts) in **one litre**.

cards.title: Sources of freshwater
body: Tap the dots to see each source.

cards.title: Two kinds of sources in Eritrea
body: Eritrea has **two** sources of freshwater. Move the slider.

states.label: Underground
states.text: **Underground sources**: deep wells (**boreholes**) and **springs**.

states.label: Surface
states.text: **Surface water**: streams, **rivers** and **dams**.

states.label: Rain fills both
states.text: Both underground and surface water are filled by **rain**. So the **main source** of water is rain.

cards.title: The main source is rain
body: Rainwater can stay on top of the ground as **surface water**,
or it can go into the ground as **underground water**.

cards.title: Measuring rainfall
body: Different parts of Eritrea get different amounts of rain.
Rainfall is measured in **millimetres (mm)**.
Places around **Asmara** get **500 mm to 700 mm** of rain in a year.

cards.title: Rainfall map of Eritrea
body: Activity 8.2. Tap the three regions. This is a simple copy of the book's map.

cards.title: Boreholes
body: In rural areas and some towns, deep wells (**boreholes**) are the main source of water.

cards.title: How a borehole gets water

steps.text: Rain falls on the ground.
The water gets into the earth. It **filters down** through sand and soft rocks until it reaches **hard rock**.
A borehole is drilled. Water is **pumped up** from the underground water basin.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: How much can a borehole give?
body: The supply from a borehole **depends on how much surface water has filtered down**.
In big towns many people live in a small area. Borehole water would **not last** very long.

cards.title: Big dams
body: In big towns rainwater must be collected in **large dams**, like the **Tokor Dam**.
One problem: a lot of dam water is **lost by evaporation**.

cards.title: Summary: sources
body: The two main sources in Eritrea: **underground water** (wells) and **surface water** (rivers, dams). Both are filled by rain.
The **central** part of Eritrea has more rain than other regions.
A country's water supply is decided by its **rain**.

cards.q: What fills both underground and surface water?
cards.why: Both are filled by rain, so rain is the main source of water.

cards.q: Which region has the highest rainfall?
cards.why: Region 1 (500 – 700 mm) is the central highland around Asmara.

cards.title: What is a cycle?
body: A **cycle** is when something goes round from one place to another and **comes back**.
The **water cycle** is a good example.

cards.title: The water cycle
body: Tap the dots to name each stage.

cards.title: Stages of the water cycle

steps.text: **A. Evaporation.** The sun's heat evaporates water from water bodies (oceans, seas) and living things. The **water vapour** rises because it is lighter than the air around it.
**B. Condensation.** As the water vapour rises it gets **cooler** and changes from gas to liquid. This forms **clouds**.
**C. Precipitation.** The wind blows the clouds higher. They become colder and heavier. The water falls as **rain**.
**D. Run-off.** The rain runs off as streams and rivers into lakes, dams or the sea. Then the cycle **starts again**.
All four together make the **water cycle**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Evaporation
body: **Evaporation** changes water slowly from a **liquid** to **water vapour** (a gas) by heat.
Warm air is lighter than cold air, so it **rises**.

cards.title: Condensation
body: **Condensation** changes water vapour (gas) back to **liquid** when it cools.
This is how **clouds** form.

cards.title: Memory trick: E-C-P-R
body: **Every Cloud Pours Rain** – and then it starts again.

cards.title: The sun drives the cycle
body: **Energy from the sun** makes water evaporate from the sea, from other water bodies and from soil surfaces.
**Plants and animals** also add water vapour to the air.

cards.title: Summary: the water cycle
body: The **water cycle** is the continuous process by which water moves through the earth and its atmosphere.
Rain returns water to the earth. It flows into water bodies and into the ground. The cycle begins **again**.

cards.q: Which of these supplies the energy that drives the water cycle?
cards.why: The sun's heat evaporates the water.

cards.q: Which place would add the most water to the cycle by evaporation?
cards.why: A warm ocean has lots of water and heat, so much water evaporates (Exercise 8.2).

cards.title: Water is not shared equally
body: The world has plenty of freshwater, but it is **not shared out equally**.
Rain does not fall evenly. Some regions are always too dry, others too wet.

cards.title: Water in Eritrea
body: Eritrea gets **not enough** rain in a year. Water supplies are not always reliable.
In a dry year surface water evaporates quickly. Rivers and dams **dry up**.
Then we must use **underground water**. If it does not rain for a long time, the water we pump up is **not replaced**.

cards.title: Water conservation
body: Keeping water and preventing it from being wasted is called **water conservation**.

cards.title: Two ways to conserve water
body: The book focuses on two methods:
a) **Collect rainwater.**
b) **Use water with care**, without wasting it.

cards.title: Rainwater tanks
body: Some homes have **rainwater tanks**.
Rain falls on the roof and flows through the **gutter** (metal pipes) to a storage tank.
The amount collected depends on the **area of the roof**.

cards.title: The rule
body: **Area of roof × rainfall = volume of water**
Change mm to m first: 1000 mm = 1 m.

cards.title: Worked example: water from a roof

steps.text: A roof is **12 m** long and **4 m** wide. **10 mm** of rain falls. How much water can we collect?
**Area** = length × width = 12 m × 4 m = **48 m²**.
**Change 10 mm to metres**: 10 ÷ 1000 = **0.01 m**.
1 m³ = 1000 L, so 0.48 × 1000 = **480 L**. That is about **24 buckets**!

body: Tap Next to follow the steps.

cards.title: Even small rain helps
body: Even from **small rainfall** a useful amount of water can be collected.

cards.title: Dams
body: On a larger scale, water is collected in **dams**.
**Mai Nefhi** and **Tokor** dams are very large. They serve the people and industries of **Asmara**.
There are also many smaller dams around the country.

cards.title: Use water with care
body: Use **less** water and **reuse** it. Move the slider.

states.label: Clothes water
states.text: Use the water left after **washing clothes** to wash the **toilet**.

states.label: Vegetable water
states.text: Use the water left after **washing vegetables** to **water plants**.

cards.title: Summary: conservation
body: To have enough clean water for everyone, we must **conserve** water.
Collect rainwater in **dams and tanks**.
Use the water we get **with care**.

cards.q: A roof has an area of 48 m². 10 mm (0.01 m) of rain falls. How much water can be collected?

cards.title: Six uses of water
body: Tap each picture.

cards.title: What do we use water for?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Drinking
states.text: All living things need water. There is **no life without water**. We also get water from food. Our body is about **70 %** water.

states.label: Keeping clean
states.text: We wash our bodies, clothes and homes. Being clean protects us from **germs and dirt**. Swimming keeps us clean and healthy, but be careful not to drown.

states.label: Growing crops
states.text: In Eritrea, farming depends on **rain**. Little rain means crops fail. Bringing water from rivers or dams to crops through pipes and channels is called **irrigation**.

states.label: Transport
states.text: Boats carry people and goods over rivers, lakes and oceans. Today ships still carry **heavy, bulky** goods like machinery, grain and oil.

states.label: Industry
states.text: Factories clean fruit and vegetables, use water as a **raw material** in soft drinks, and clean factories. **Most** industrial water is used for **cooling**.

states.label: Home for living things
states.text: Plants and animals live in water. Fish taken out of the river or sea **die**.

cards.title: Our body
body: Our body is made up of about **70 % water**.

cards.title: Irrigation
body: **Irrigation**: water from rivers or dams reaches the crops through **pipes and channels**.

cards.title: Industry and cooling
body: Most water used by industry is for **cooling**.
Example: water cools the steam used to make electric power from fuels.

cards.title: Memory trick: six uses
body: **Dad Cleans Carrots, Then Irons Hats.**

cards.title: Summary: uses
body: People need water for **drinking, cooking and washing**.
Water is needed for **agriculture, industry, transport and electricity**, and as a **home** for living things.

cards.q: Most of the water used by industry is used for:
cards.why: The textbook says most industrial water is for cooling.

cards.title: Clean water and germs
body: Some water has harmful **micro-organisms**.
Micro-organisms are **very small living things**, like **bacteria**.
In dirty (**contaminated**) water they cause **diseases**. So dirty water is **not safe** to drink.

cards.title: How river water gets dirty
body: River water may start as rain, then run across **dirty** places.
It can be contaminated by **urine or faeces** of animals or people, or by **industrial waste**.

cards.title: Five ways we make water dirty
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Water becomes contaminated when we…
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Rubbish
states.text: …throw **rubbish** into the water or near it.

states.label: Toilet
states.text: …**urinate or defecate** near or into a source of water.

states.label: Washing
states.text: …**wash** our bodies or clothes in it.

states.label: Animals
states.text: …allow **animals** to drink from the water.

states.label: Containers
states.text: …use **dirty containers** to collect water.

cards.title: Rules for safe water (Activity 8.5)
head: Rule
Do or don't?
rows: Urinate or defecate into sources of water.
Put hands in a water container.
Throw rubbish into sources of water.

cards.title: Water-borne diseases
body: Every year **millions** of people die from **water-borne diseases**.
Three of them are **diarrhoea**, **bilharzia** and **cholera**.
They are serious and **spread easily**.

cards.title: Memory trick: D-B-C
body: **Dirty Bad Cup** = three water-borne diseases.

cards.title: Two jobs
body: Making water safe = **1. make it clean** (remove dirt) + **2. kill harmful germs**.

cards.title: Filtration with a cloth
body: Activity 8.6. Move the slider.

states.label: Before
states.text: In the small beaker the water is **muddy**.

states.label: After
states.text: Pour it through a **clean cloth**. The water below looks **cleaner**. But it may still have germs.

cards.title: Filtration
body: Sand and other solid particles can be removed by **filtration**.
A cloth filter is only good for **small** amounts of water.
**Sand filtering** cleans small and large amounts.

cards.title: A sand filter
body: Activity 8.7. A cut bottle, upside down. Tap the layers.

steps.text: Cut a large plastic bottle. Make small holes in the cap with a nail. Turn it upside down.
Put **stones** at the bottom, then **coarse sand**, then **fine sand** on top.
Pour dirty water at the top. The dirt is **trapped** in the sand and stones.
The first water may be dirty. Keep pouring until the water comes out **clean**.

cards.title: Borehole water
body: Borehole water is usually **clean and safe** to drink.
It has been **filtered through the ground** and has no harmful micro-organisms.

cards.title: Decanting

steps.text: Pour muddy water into a beaker.
Let it stand. The sand and dirt **settle** at the bottom. This solid is called **sediment**.
Carefully pour the **clear water** at the top into another container. This is **decanting**.

body: Activity 8.8. Tap Next.

cards.title: Clean-looking is not always safe
body: Filtered or decanted water may **look clean**, but it can still have harmful micro-organisms.
To make it **safe**, we must **kill** them.

cards.title: Two ways to kill germs
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Boiling
states.text: Boil water for **10 to 15 minutes**. Boiling kills micro-organisms. Always boil water from open wells and rivers, and all water for **young babies**.

states.label: Chlorine
states.text: **Chlorine** is a poisonous gas, but a **small amount** kills germs in drinking water. Adding chlorine to water is called **chlorination**.

cards.title: Products and features
body: Tap each dot.

cards.title: Two groups
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Products
states.text: **Products** of the earth: **water**, **living things** and **mineral resources** (oil, coal, metals, stone, sand).

states.label: Features
states.text: **Features** of the earth: **land**, **air**, **sunshine** and **climate**.

cards.title: Renewable or non-renewable?
body: Natural resources are **renewable** or **non-renewable**. Move the slider.

states.label: Renewable
states.text: **Renewable** resources are replaced by natural processes in **100 years or less**. Examples: **air, water, soil, living things**. Air, water and soil are recycled by nature. Living things reproduce.

states.label: Non-renewable
states.text: **Non-renewable** resources **cannot** be replaced within 100 years. Examples: mineral fuels like **oil and coal**. People are using them up.

cards.title: 100 years
body: Replaced in **100 years or less** → renewable.
**Not** replaced within 100 years → non-renewable.

cards.title: Memory trick: renewable
body: Renewable: **Always We See Life** (air, water, soil, living things).

cards.title: When a resource gets scarce
body: Scientists believe people can never use up **all** the resources. People can:
- **substitute** (use another resource instead): **aluminium** in place of **copper**, because copper is scarce but aluminium compounds are plenty.
- **reuse** it: bits of used **iron** are melted and used again to make **steel**.
- use **alternative energy** like **solar** or **nuclear** energy after mineral fuels are finished.

cards.title: Uses of natural resources
body: Natural resources are used to make **food**, **fuel**, and **raw materials** for finished goods.
All our food comes from **plants and animals**.
Most plants and animals need **air, sunshine, soil and water**.
People burn **wood** from trees for fuel.
**Minerals** are raw materials for cars, plastics and refrigerators.

cards.q: Which resources cannot be replaced in a short period of time?
cards.why: Mineral fuels like oil and coal cannot be replaced within 100 years.

cards.title: A candle in a tin can

steps.text: Activity 9.2: put a burning candle inside a tin can with a small hole. Cover the top with a metal or glass plate.
Look under the cover. A **black layer** forms. The book explains later: when fuels burn without enough air, they make **smoke** with small particles of **carbon (soot)**.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Our environment
body: Our physical environment is made of **air, water and land (soil)**.
Plants and animals need all of these to live and grow.

cards.title: What is pollution?
body: **Pollution** is the addition of any outside material that **disturbs the natural balance** of air, soil and water.
It makes the environment **unsuitable for life**.

cards.title: Pollutant
body: A **pollutant** is any material that can **harm living things** by polluting the environment.

cards.title: Man-made or natural?
body: Causes of pollution can be **man-made** or **natural**. Move the slider.

states.label: Man-made
states.text: **Man-made** causes: **industrial wastes**, **burning fuels**. Figure 9.1 also shows cutting trees and spraying chemicals.

states.label: Natural
states.text: **Natural** causes: **volcanic eruption**, **forest fire**, **dust storm** and **flood**.

cards.title: Three kinds of pollution
body: At this level you learn **three** kinds:
**A.** soil pollution, **B.** water pollution, **C.** air pollution.

cards.title: What is soil?
body: **Soil** is the thin layer of organic and inorganic materials that covers the earth's rocky surface. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Parts of soil
body: The **organic** part comes from **decayed remains** of plants and animals. It is mostly in the **top soil**.
The **inorganic** part is **rock fragments**.
Soil forms over **thousands of years** by **weathering** of rocks.

cards.title: Soil pollution
body: **Soil pollution** is adding energy, organisms or substances to the soil that **change its quality**.
It harms the normal use of soil and endangers **public health** and other living things.

cards.title: Four main causes of soil pollution
body: Tap each one.

cards.title: The four causes
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Soil erosion
states.text: **Soil erosion**: soil particles are carried away by **wind or water**. Humans speed it up by **building, mining, cutting trees, farming** and **overgrazing**.

states.label: Fertilizers
states.text: **Artificial fertilizers** add extra nutrients and increase crop yield. But **large amounts** may stop soil bacteria from decaying wastes and making nutrients naturally.

states.label: Pesticides
states.text: **Pesticides** are chemicals that **kill pests**: unwanted animals and plants on crops.

states.label: Solid waste
states.text: **Solid waste** is whatever people throw away: garbage, refuse and harmful chemicals from homes and industries.

cards.title: Where plants get their food
body: Plants get **carbon, hydrogen and oxygen** from **air and water**.
They get other nutrients from the **soil**.

cards.title: Four types of pesticides
body: Pesticides are named by the pest they control. Move the slider.

states.label: Insecticides
states.text: **Insecticides** stop damage by **insects**.

states.label: Herbicides
states.text: **Herbicides** kill **weeds**: plants growing where they are not wanted.

states.label: Fungicides
states.text: **Fungicides** control **fungi** that cause plant diseases.

states.label: Rodenticides
states.text: **Rodenticides** control **rats and mice**.

cards.title: Memory trick: I-H-F-R
body: **Insects Hate Farmers' Rules.**

cards.title: The story of DDT
body: **DDT** was the first widely used **insecticide**. It seemed perfect.
But insects became **resistant** to it, and it did **not decompose** easily. It stayed in the environment.
Large birds of prey like **ospreys, falcons and eagles** became **endangered**.

cards.title: Pesticides build up in a food chain

steps.text: Most pesticides break down quickly. But **persistent** ones stay a long time. They get into soil, plants and small organisms.
Animals higher up (like livestock and fish) eat **many** of the lower ones and collect the chemical.
Birds eat many fish. They get **even more** of the chemical.
The highest organism, like **human beings**, gets the **most**. It can cause **health problems**.

body: Figure 9.2. Watch the red dots grow.

cards.title: Harm from solid waste
body: Harmful chemicals cause many **birth defects**, **cancer**, and **respiratory, nervous and kidney** diseases.
Most solid waste in towns is **recyclable** or **biodegradable**.

cards.title: Clean water in nature
body: A natural water body has a **balance** of plant and animal life.
Useful **bacteria** digest waste. Fish use the **dissolved oxygen** in water.
Absolutely pure water does not exist in nature: many substances are dissolved in it.

cards.title: Water pollution
body: **Unwanted substances** in water cause **water pollution**.
These substances are **pollutants**.

cards.title: Five man-made water pollutants
body: Tap the dots.

cards.title: Where do they come from?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Excreta and dung
states.text: In rural areas, **human excreta and animal dung** are washed into water sources.

states.label: Industrial wastes
states.text: From chemical companies, **mining**, paper mills, breweries and slaughterhouses.

states.label: Fertilizers
states.text: Fertilizers in the soil are washed by running water into the **sea**.

states.label: Detergents
states.text: From washing **clothes and dishes**.

states.label: Oil spill
states.text: From **factories and ships**.

cards.title: Dangers of polluted water
body: It may contain harmful **worms and micro-organisms**.
They cause **cholera, diarrhoea, dysentery, typhoid** and **jaundice**.
Too much untreated **sewage** makes bacteria multiply. They use up the oxygen, so **fish cannot survive**.

cards.title: Treating drinking water
body: Drinking water must have **no pollutants**.
It should be **filtered** and treated with **chlorine** to kill bacteria.
In some areas a trace of **sodium fluoride** is added to reduce **tooth decay**.

cards.title: Air pollution
body: Air pollution turns clear, odourless air into **hazy, smelly** air.
It **harms health**, **kills plants** and **damages property**.
People pollute the air by **burning** things.

cards.title: Smoke
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Incomplete burning
states.text: **Incomplete burning** of fuel makes a lot of **smoke**. Smoke has small particles of carbon (**soot**). Buildings get dirty and old faster.

states.label: Enough oxygen
states.text: With enough **oxygen** from the air, the fuel burns well with **no smoke**.

cards.title: Smoke and our health
body: Smoke burns the **eyes** and irritates the **lungs**.
Particles can settle in the lungs and make **asthma, bronchitis** and **pneumonia** worse.

cards.title: Gases and rainwater
body: Burning fuels also gives off **unpleasant gases**. They can **kill plants**.
Rain dissolves these gases, so **rainwater** may not be as pure as you think.

cards.title: Traffic
body: Car and lorry **exhausts** pollute the air in cities.
Old engines make unpleasant smoke.
All vehicles give out **carbon monoxide (CO)**, a **very poisonous** gas.

cards.title: Sources of air pollution
body: Figure 9.4: most gases and particles in polluted air come from **burning**. Tap the dots.

cards.title: Burning and what it gives off
head: Source
Pollutants

cards.q: Which of these is a natural cause of pollution?
cards.why: Volcanic eruption, forest fire, dust storm and flood are natural causes.

cards.q: Harmful bacteria in tap water are killed by:
cards.why: Chlorine kills bacteria. Fluoride is for teeth; filtering removes solids.

cards.title: What is global warming?
body: **Global warming** is the **rise in the average temperature** of the earth,
because gases released into the atmosphere **keep heat** in.

cards.title: Three processes that release the gases
body: 1. **Burning forests** to clear land for farms, roads and cities releases **carbon dioxide**.
2. **Burning fuels** (petrol, coal, natural gas) in houses, factories and vehicles releases **carbon dioxide**.
3. Hot **engines of vehicles** release **oxides of nitrogen**.

cards.title: Memory trick: F-F-E
body: **F**orests, **F**uels, **E**ngines.

cards.title: What scientists predict
body: Too much **carbon dioxide** and **oxides of nitrogen** trap heat. Move the slider.

states.label: Heat trapped
states.text: The gases **trap heat** in the air, making the earth **warmer**.

states.label: Ice melts
states.text: **Ice at the poles melts.** The sea level rises and **floods** cities near the sea.

states.label: Drought
states.text: Some places get **less rain**, causing **drought**.

states.label: Deserts grow
states.text: The boundaries of **deserts expand**.

cards.title: Two gases
body: The gases that trap heat: **carbon dioxide** and **oxides of nitrogen**.

cards.title: Summary: pollution and warming
body: Pollution disturbs the natural balance of air, soil and water.
Three kinds: **soil, water, air** pollution.
Global warming comes from **burning forests**, **burning fuels** and **hot vehicle engines**.

cards.q: Which of these is a consequence of global warming?

options.B: melting of ice at the poles

cards.why: Scientists predict polar ice will melt and the sea will rise.

cards.q: Which releases gases that cause global warming?
cards.why: Both release carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which resources cannot be replaced in a short period of time?
why: Oil and coal (mineral fuels) cannot be replaced within 100 years (p. 187).
Plants, water and animals are renewable.
questions.tip: Fuels from the ground = non-renewable.

similar.q: Give two renewable resources.
similar.a: e.g. air and water (also soil, living things)

Burning fuels like petrol releases carbon dioxide (p. 196).
So both A and B.
