questions.q: A consequence of global warming is:

options.B: melting of ice at the poles
options.D: increase of oxygen in the atmosphere

why: Scientists predict ice at the poles will melt and the sea will rise (p. 197).
The book says some places get LESS rain, so C is wrong.
questions.tip: Warmer → ice melts.

similar.q: Give one more consequence of global warming.
similar.a: drought in some places, or deserts expanding

questions.q: Pollution is caused by:
why: Causes can be man-made (human activities) or natural (volcanoes, dust storms) (p. 189).
So all three.
questions.tip: Man-made AND natural.

similar.q: Name two natural causes of pollution.

questions.q: The inorganic portion of the soil is made up of:
why: The inorganic part is made of rock fragments (p. 191).
Decayed remains are the organic part.
questions.tip: Inorganic = not from living things = rock.

similar.q: Where is the organic part of soil concentrated?

questions.q: The main pollutant of air is:
why: People pollute air by burning, which makes a lot of smoke (p. 195).
Smoke makes air dirty, burns eyes and irritates lungs.
questions.tip: Think of what you see from burning.

similar.q: What is in smoke that makes buildings dirty?

questions.q: Harmful bacteria in tap water are killed by:
why: Water should be treated with chlorine to kill bacteria (p. 195).
Fluoride is for teeth; filtering removes solids.
questions.tip: Chlorine kills; fluoride for teeth.

similar.q: Why is sodium fluoride added to water in some areas?

questions.q: ___ is the addition of any external material that disturbs the natural balance of air, soil and water.
why: This is the book's definition of pollution (p. 189).
questions.tip: Disturbs the natural balance = pollution.

similar.q: What is a pollutant?
similar.a: any material that can harm living things by polluting the environment

questions.q: The gases that trap heat in the air, making the earth warmer, are carbon dioxide and ___.
why: Too much carbon dioxide and oxides of nitrogen trap heat (p. 197).
questions.tip: Two gases: CO₂ and oxides of nitrogen.

similar.q: What is the warming of the earth by trapped heat called?

questions.q: Plants obtain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from air and ___.
why: Plants get carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from air and water (p. 191).
Other nutrients come from the soil.
questions.tip: C, H, O come from air and water.

similar.q: What can large amounts of fertilizer do to soil bacteria?
similar.a: decrease their ability to decay wastes and make nutrients naturally

questions.q: Name the four most widely used types of pesticides and what each controls.
questions.answer: Insecticides (insects), herbicides (weeds), fungicides (fungi that cause plant diseases), rodenticides (rats and mice).
why: The book lists these four on p. 191 – 192.
questions.tip: Insects Hate Farmers' Rules.

similar.q: Why did birds like eagles become endangered?
similar.a: DDT did not decompose and persisted in the environment.

questions.q: Explain how pesticides affect the health of human beings.
questions.answer: Persistent pesticides stay in the environment. Lower organisms absorb them; higher organisms eat many of them and collect more. Humans at the top get the most, which can cause health problems.
why: Persistent pesticides do not break down (p. 192).
Each level eats many of the level below.
The amount grows until the top – human beings.
questions.tip: Follow the food chain: the top gets the most.

similar.q: Do most pesticides stay a long time?
similar.a: No, most decompose after a short time; only persistent ones stay.

questions.q: Write the effects of smoke, and say how to reduce smoke when burning wood or fuel.
questions.answer: Smoke makes air and buildings dirty (they age faster), burns eyes, irritates lungs and worsens asthma, bronchitis and pneumonia. Give enough oxygen (air) so the fuel burns efficiently with no smoke.
why: Effects of smoke on p. 195.
With enough oxygen, fuel burns with no smoke (p. 195).
questions.tip: Smoke comes from incomplete burning → give more air.

similar.q: What very poisonous gas do all vehicles give out?

units.title: Sound
units.intro: This unit is about how sound is made, how it travels, how fast it goes, how animals hear, and echoes.

u10speed.title: Speed of sound in some substances

u10speed_q.title: Speed of sound in some substances (quiz)

cards.title: Activity 10.1: a ruler on a desk

steps.text: Hold a 30 cm ruler under a book on the edge of a desk. Most of it sticks out.
Pull the free end down and let it go.
It moves **up and down** quickly. You **hear a sound**.
Touch it so it stops moving. The sound **stops** too.

body: Tap Next.

cards.title: Feel your throat
body: Put your fingers gently on your throat and speak.
You feel your throat **vibrate**. This is how your voice is made.

cards.title: How sound is made
body: A **vibration** is a backward and forward, or up and down, movement of an object.
**Sound is produced by objects that vibrate.**

cards.title: Sources of sound
body: **Vibrating objects are sources of sound.** Tap the dots.

cards.title: One vibration
body: Look at the ruler again. It starts at point **B**.
**One vibration** is a complete movement from **B to A and back to B**.

cards.title: Frequency
body: **Frequency** is the number of **complete vibrations** in **one second**.
It is measured in **hertz (Hz)**, named after the German scientist **Heinrich Hertz**.
**1 Hz = 1 complete vibration per second.**

cards.title: Count the vibrations
body: Move the slider. Count the waves in one second.

states.label: 1 Hz
states.text: One complete vibration each second is **1 Hz**.

states.label: 3 Hz
states.text: Three vibrations each second is **3 Hz**.

states.label: 7 Hz
states.text: A guitar string that vibrates 7 times in one second has a frequency of **7 Hz**.

cards.title: Example
body: An object vibrates **50 times** in one second.
That is 50 vibrations per second, so its frequency is **50 Hz**.

cards.title: Who hears what?
body: Animals can only hear sounds of certain frequencies. Move the slider.

states.label: Humans
states.text: **Humans** normally hear from **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz** (20 kHz).

states.label: Dogs
states.text: **Dogs** hear from **20 Hz to 35 kHz**: higher sounds than we can.

states.label: Bats
states.text: **Bats** hear from **20 Hz to 160 000 Hz**.

cards.title: kilo means 1000
body: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz, so 20 kHz = 20 000 Hz and 35 kHz = 35 000 Hz.

cards.q: A bird sings at 60 vibrations per second. Its frequency is:
cards.why: Vibrations per second = hertz, so 60 Hz.

cards.q: What are the lowest and highest frequencies dogs can hear?
cards.why: Dogs hear from 20 Hz to 35 kHz.

cards.title: Sound in air (Activity 10.2)
body: A pupil claps two metal lids at one end of the playground.
Pupils at the other end **hear** it. Sound travels through **air** (a gas).

cards.title: Sound in a solid (Activity 10.3)
body: Make a **string telephone**: two tin cans joined by a tight 5 m string, held by nails.
Your friend speaks into one can. You hear through the other.
Sound travels through the **string** (a solid).

cards.title: Sound in a liquid (Activity 10.4)
body: Hit two stones together in a bucket of **water**.
Put your ear close to the bucket. You hear it. Sound travels through **water** (a liquid).

cards.title: Solids, liquids and gases
body: Tap each panel.

cards.title: Medium
body: The substance that sound travels through is called a **medium**.
Sound can travel through **solids, liquids and gases**.
Sound **needs** a medium.

cards.title: Where can sound go?
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Gas
states.text: Sound travels through **air**.

states.label: Solid
states.text: Sound travels through a **solid**, like a string.

states.label: Liquid
states.text: Sound travels through a **liquid**, like water.

states.label: Vacuum
states.text: A **vacuum** is a space with **no particles**. There is no medium, so sound **cannot** travel.

cards.title: Why not in a vacuum?
body: Sound is caused by **vibrating particles**.
A vacuum has **no particles**, so nothing can vibrate and carry the sound.

cards.title: Memory trick: S-L-G, not V
body: **S**ound **L**oves **G**oing – but never through a **V**acuum.

cards.q: Which one is NOT a medium for sound?
cards.why: A vacuum has no particles, so sound cannot travel through it.

cards.title: Starting pistol
body: At a 400 m race the teacher fires the starting pistol. Move the slider.

states.label: See
states.text: Runners **see** the smoke first.

states.label: Hear
states.text: They **hear** the sound a little later. Light and sound travel at **different speeds**.

cards.title: Other examples
body: You see an axe hit the wood before you hear it.
In a thunderstorm you see **lightning** before you hear **thunder**.

cards.title: Speed of sound
body: **Speed = distance travelled ÷ time taken**
v = s ÷ t (v = speed, s = distance, t = time)

cards.title: Light or sound?
head: Speed in air
body: Light is **much faster** than sound.

cards.title: Different substances
body: Sound travels at different speeds in different substances.
Generally sound is **fastest in solids**, slower in **liquids**, and **slowest in air**.

cards.title: Table 1
body: Tap each bar.

cards.title: Memory trick: fastest first
body: From fastest to slowest: **S – L – G**.

cards.title: Worked example 1: find the speed
cards.problem: Two people stand 200 m apart. One fires a pistol. The other hears it after 0.6 s. Find the speed of sound in air.

steps.text: Given: s = 200 m, t = 0.6 s. Required: v.

cards.title: Worked example 2: find the distance
cards.problem: Sound travels at about 330 m/s in air. How far does it go in 10 s?

steps.text: From v = s ÷ t we get s = v × t.

cards.title: Thunder and lightning sum
body: Sound speed 340 m/s. Thunder heard **20 s** after lightning.
Distance = 340 × 20 = **6800 m** away.

cards.q: The speed of sound in a liquid is ___ than in air.
cards.why: Sound travels faster through liquids than through air.

cards.q: A gun is fired 1020 m away. Sound speed is 340 m/s. How long until you hear it?
cards.why: t = s ÷ v = 1020 ÷ 340 = 3 s. You see the flash almost at once.

cards.title: Ears like ours
body: In Grade 6 you learned how the human ear works.
Many animals have ears **like ours** and hear sound in a similar way.

cards.title: Big outer ears
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Animals
states.text: **Dogs, cats and donkeys** have **large outer ears**. The larger the outer ears, the **better** the animal hears. Some find their **food** by listening.

states.label: Paper cones
states.text: Activity 10.5: hold paper cones at your ears and listen to pupils talking. Then listen without them and compare. The cones act like **large outer ears**.

cards.title: The rule
body: **The larger the outer ears, the better the animals hear.**

cards.title: Summary: animal hearing
body: Many animals hear like humans.
Many animals have outer ears; big outer ears help them hear better.

cards.q: What is the advantage of large outer ears?
cards.why: The larger the outer ears, the better the animal hears.

cards.title: Echo
body: When sound hits hard objects like **bare walls** and **cliffs**, it travels back (**reflects**).
A **reflected sound** is called an **echo**.

cards.title: How an echo forms
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Sound goes out
states.text: You shout. The sound travels to the wall.

states.label: It comes back
states.text: The sound **bounces back** like a ball off a wall. You hear an **echo**.

states.label: Activity 10.6
states.text: One tube points a ticking watch at the wall. Another tube at your ear points at the wall. When you hear the ticking, measure the angles of the two tubes to the wall and compare them.

cards.title: Like light
body: Reflection of sound is **much like reflection of light**.
Shouting in a school or sports hall makes **lots of echoes**.

cards.title: Animals use echoes
body: **Dolphins** and **bats** make sounds and listen for the echoes. Move the slider.

states.label: Send
states.text: The bat makes a sound.

states.label: Listen
states.text: The echo comes back. It tells the bat **how far away** the object is. This helps them **find their way and hunt**.

cards.title: Echoes can be a problem
body: Echoes cause problems in **halls, cinemas, music, radio and television studios**.

cards.title: Reducing echoes
body: Move the slider.

states.label: Hard walls
states.text: **Smooth, hard** surfaces are **good reflectors** of sound: lots of echoes.

states.label: Soft materials
states.text: Cover walls with **soft, thick materials** (fibreboards) and **heavy curtains**; cover floors with **thick carpets**. Soft surfaces **absorb** sound, so echoes are not produced.

cards.q: Echoes are caused by the ___ of sound.
cards.why: An echo is a reflected sound.

tips.text: Sound = vibration. No vibration, no sound.
Frequency in Hz = vibrations per second. 7 vibrations in 1 s → 7 Hz.
Humans 20 Hz – 20 kHz; dogs 20 Hz – 35 kHz; bats 20 Hz – 160 000 Hz.
Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases – never through a vacuum.

Sound can travel through a vacuum.

Humans hear up to 20 000 Hz.

items.why: Solids are fastest: steel 5940 m/s, air 343 m/s.

items.text: Bats and dolphins use echoes to hunt.
Soft materials are good reflectors of sound.
items.why: Soft materials absorb sound.

questions.q: Which one of the following is not a medium?
why: Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases (p. 207).
A vacuum has no particles, so it is not a medium.
questions.tip: No particles = no medium.

similar.q: Name three mediums sound can travel through.
similar.a: solids, liquids and gases (e.g. string, water, air)

questions.q: A guitar string makes 7 vibrations in one second. Its frequency is:
why: Frequency = number of complete vibrations in one second.
7 vibrations in 1 s = 7 Hz.
questions.tip: Per second → just read the number.

similar.q: What does a frequency of 10 Hz mean?

questions.q: The normal human ear can hear sounds with frequencies from:
why: Humans hear from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, which is 20 kHz (p. 204).
questions.tip: Twenty to twenty thousand.

similar.q: What is the hearing range of bats?

questions.q: The order in which sound travels in wood, gas and water, from fastest to slowest, is:
why: Wood is a solid, water is a liquid, gas is a gas.
Sound is fastest in solids, then liquids, slowest in gases (p. 208).
questions.tip: Solid → liquid → gas.

similar.q: In Table 1, which is faster: glass or water?

questions.q: Sound is produced by ___, such as a ticking clock.
why: Sound is produced by objects that vibrate (p. 203).
questions.tip: Sound = vibration.

similar.q: What do you feel on your throat when you speak?

questions.q: ___ is measured in hertz (Hz).
why: Frequency is measured in hertz, after Heinrich Hertz (p. 204).
questions.tip: Hertz → frequency.

similar.q: Who was hertz named after?

questions.q: Sound travels faster in ___ than in liquids.
why: Generally sound travels faster through solids than through air or liquids (p. 208).
questions.tip: Solids first.

similar.q: Is sound faster in liquids or in air?

questions.q: The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Thunder is heard 20 seconds after the lightning. How far away is the storm?
why: s = v × t
questions.tip: Distance = speed × time.

similar.q: Sound in air is 330 m/s. How far in 10 s?

questions.q: A gun is fired 1020 m away. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, what is the time difference between seeing the flash and hearing the sound?
why: Light arrives almost at once (3 × 10⁸ m/s).
Time for sound: t = s ÷ v = 1020 m ÷ 340 m/s = 3 s.
So the difference is about 3 s.
questions.tip: Time = distance ÷ speed.

similar.q: Two people 200 m apart; sound takes 0.6 s. Speed?

questions.q: The speed of sound through water is 1500 m/s. How far will sound travel through water in 5 seconds?
why: s = v × t
questions.tip: Multiply speed by time.

similar.q: How far does sound go in steel (5940 m/s) in 2 s?

questions.q: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum?
questions.answer: Sound is caused by vibrating particles. A vacuum has no particles, so there is no medium to carry the sound.
why: Sound needs a medium (p. 207).
A vacuum is a space with no particles.
questions.tip: No particles → nothing to vibrate.

similar.q: What is a medium?
similar.a: the substance through which sound travels

questions.q: Why do some rooms make an echo? What can be done to solve the problem?
questions.answer: Bare, smooth, hard walls and floors reflect sound. Cover walls with soft, thick materials (fibreboards) and heavy curtains, and cover floors with thick carpets; these absorb sound.
why: Smooth, hard surfaces are good reflectors (p. 213).
Soft surfaces absorb sound and prevent reflection.
questions.tip: Hard reflects; soft absorbs.

similar.q: Name two animals that use echoes.

questions.q: Describe a simple observation that shows sound travels much more slowly than light.
questions.answer: At a race the starting pistol is fired: runners see the smoke first and hear the bang some seconds later. (Also: lightning is seen before thunder is heard.)
why: The textbook's starting-pistol example (p. 208).
Light is 3 × 10⁸ m/s; sound only about 330 m/s.
questions.tip: See first, hear later.

similar.q: In a thunderstorm, which comes first: thunder or lightning?
